speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I would like to call the attention of the House to some statements which were made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) in my absence on Friday last. The statement of the hon. member for Rouville, which is to be found on page 3,592 of 'Hansard,' is as follows:
I do not wish to offer any objection to the Bill, but I might remind the House and the leader of the Government that the Minister of Justice is more generous than the Postmaster General. Three years ago a mail carrier perished in trying to save the mails during a storm on lake of Two Mountains, between Ottawa and Montreal. He left a widow and five or six children. The case was brought to the notice of the House by the hon member for Two Mountains (Mr. Ethier). He begged the Government to do something for the widow and children, but the minister refused. More than that, the people of Oka petitioned the Postmaster General to transfer the mail contract, formerly held by her husband to the widow of this man. The petition was turned down, the widow has received nothing, and there she is to-day.
On page 3,593 I find -the following:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: I agree with the minister in everything he has said, but I would strongly recommend to him the case brought to his attention by the hon. member for Eouville. It is not in his department, I know, but the circumstances are very much the same. Here is a man who lost his life in the performance of his duty. The circumstances may not have been heroic, but, after all, the case is deserving of attention from the State, which has benefited by the performance of this man's duty. If the hon. minister could prevail on his neighbour, the Postmaster General, to do the same for this man's widow, he would win the gratitude not only of the widow but of every member in this House.
Mr. Doherty: I shall be very glad to call his attention to what has been said.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: Calling his attention to it will not accomplish much.
As I said, tho.se statements were made in my absence. A.s a matter of fact, I asked Parliament to vote $1,000 for this
poor woman, and that amount has been voted and paid. Moreover, much against the wishes of many of my political friends, I got this woman appointed as postmistress at that place; and I have received from her letters expressing her most profound gratitude. In one sentence of the letter 1 have in my hand she .says:
. It seems to me that I have suffered enough since that time without having people heap reproaches on my benefactor after what he has done for me.
These are the facts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As far as I am concerned, I spoke under a misapprehension, and I am very glad to offer my congratulations to the Postmaster General on what he has done.

I was away during the first session of this Parliament, but I gathered from certain remarks that the hon. Postmaster General had refused the request of the member for Two Mountains. I, also, am glad to congratulate the Postmaster General on what he has done.

speechtext:
The House in Committee on Bill No. 150, to Incorporate the Prudential Life of Canada.-Mr. Niokle. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 10:
The new company shall not commence business until at least one hundred thousand dollars have been paid upon its capital stock.

When I intervened on
Friday night to say a word about this Bill, it was not with any desire to prevent its passing but to draw attention to the wording of section 10 which was discussed before the Committee on Banking and Commerce. It was contended 'by certain members of that committee that the language of the clause is not clear; that it might be complied with by showing that one hundred thousand dollars of capital had been subscribed at some time in the past, but that might now be impaired to some extent, and that it was necessary to have the clause so clear that there should be no doubt that one hundred thousand dollars of capital would be to the fore when the company is being incorporated with a federal charter. Apart from any undertaking of the Finance Department which no doubt will be carried out, I would like to know if the minister thinks the language of the clause is sufficiently clear as it stands to enjoin the department to see that there is one hundred thousand dollars to the good now, before the company would be chartered for business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Since this matter
was last under discussion, I have made inquiry as to the Dominion Acts passed during the last three years incorporating companies with the power of taking over provincial companies. I find that in 1911 there were two companies so incorporated: The Merchants and Employers Guarantee Accident Company, and the Continental Fire Insurance Company of Canada; in 1912 there was incorporated the Liverpool-Manitoba Assurance Company, and in 1913 the Canadian Provident Insurance Company, the Underwriters Corporation of Canada, and the Western Canada Accident and Guarantee Insurance Company. The Insurance Department informs me that while these Acts prescribe the amount of capital stock required to be paid up before the new company shall commence the transaction of its several classes of business, there is no provision in any of these Acts regarding the amount of unimpaired capital to be shown. There is a provision

in each of these Acts that there shall be a certain paid-up capital, but there is no specific provision that there shall be an excess of assets over liabilities, or an unimpaired capital. The Department of Insurance further informs me that in practice they have always insisted, before a license is granted, that the amount of paid-up capital mentioned in the Act of incorporation shall be wholly unimpaired. I have here the Acts incorporating the several companies which I have mentioned, but I do not think it necessary to go into them in detail. My hon. friend from Guysborough will observe that a new company is being incorporated under this Bill, H-2 of the Senate, that is to say, it is a new incorporation. This new company is to have the power of taking over an old company, the Prudential Life Insurance Company, incorporated under the statutes of the Province of Manitoba. By section 10 of the Act it is provided that the new company shall not commence business until at least one hundred thousand dollars has been paid upon its capital stock. That section is on all fours with sections in these several Bills which I have mentioned, passed during tli-e last three years. When the matter was under discussion in the committee, I stated that it might be conceivable that a new company might have one hundred thousand dollars of fully paid-up stock and yet there might not be a surplus of one hundred thousand dollars of assets over liabilities, and therefore, if there had been no other circumstances in the matter it would have been entirely agreeable to me that the amount of sixty-five thousand dollar's-which had been fixed in a Bill passed a little while ago by the committee- or eighty thousand dollars, or a hundred thousand dollars, should have been provided as the amount of unimpaired capital, the company should show before being licensed to carry on its business. But by reason of the considerations which were drawn to the attention of the committee, namely, that this Bill had been strongly opposed on the ground of its name; that last year it had been rejected in the Senate; that this year it had passed the Senate and that the change now might involve, by reason of the lateness of the session, the company not obtaining inoorporationj at all, it appeared to me that if the mat* ter could be safe-guarded, as it can be safeguarded, by the Insurance Department, it would not be necessary to insert in this Bill a provision which has not in the past

been usual in connection with similar incorporations. These being the tacts it would appear to me that the matter of the standing of the company and its solvency is safeguarded by the precautions I have taken in instructing the Insurance Department to see that before the license is granted the company shall have an unimpaired fully-paid-up capital of one hundred thousand dollars. I may say that at the last meeting of the Banking and Commerce Committee, I was assured by the manager and by the president of the Prudential Life Insurance Company, that they have no objection whatever to taking that course and would have no difficulty in complying with the requirement of the department.

Another question. The minister in his letter to the superintendent of insurance says that he should associate with his officers an outside actuary to make an investigation into this company. I would like to know who is to pay for the services of an outside actuary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not consider that aspect of it, but personally I would see no objection to the Insurance Department paying. That will be done in the ordinary course of business. It is not unusual for the department to engage expert officials from outside in connection with the conduct of public business devolving upon it.
I think the Prudential Life Company should pay for the outside actuary; of course the actuaries of the department will do the work as part of the business of their office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would suggest to my hon. friend that perhaps it would be better that the Government should pay, for the reason that my idea in suggesting that outside actuarial assistance be obtained was in order to put the matter of the standing of the company beyond any question. If a company whose affairs are to be investigated pay for the actuary, it might be suggested that the actuary, being so paid by the company, might not be as strict as if he were paid by the Government. It would occur to me that the proper way of dealing with the matter would be for the Insurance Department to pay for any actuarial assistance which might be obtained.

I do not regard it as important. I have no doubt at all that the minister will make the necessary investigation, and that everything will be done
carefully and in order. I have every confidence in the minister and the department that this matter wall be attended to as he states it will be. This measure is now practically a Government measure, and the minister, of course, takes the responsibility in regard to it.
The point that I wish to impress upon the House is that the House has functions in regard to these matters as well as the Department of Finance, and that it cannot discharge its functions by passing them over to the department. It is well understand that the functions of the Department of Finance are administrative and that the functions of the House are legislative. It is the duty of the Department of Finance to issue a license to a company when it complies with the terms of the charter granted by this House. If the House chooses to grant a charter to a company to do insurance business in Canada with a capital of $5,000, and if the company comes next day knocking at the door of the Department of Finance with the charter, complying with the terms of it and furnishing the $5,000 capital, or the proof of it, it is the duty of the department to issue the license, notwithstanding that the minister may be of the opinion that the company ought to have at least $100,000 capital. Therefore it is important that the House in all these matters should provide clearly and distinctly what is required because, as to what is required, the Department of Finance will carry out the mandate of the House. It is especially important, when we remember the unfortunate incident which took place recently in regard to the Union Life and incidents of a similar nature. Therefore I hope the minister will see the point which I make, namely, that in all these charters that are granted it is proper and right that the House should be clear and distinct in regard to the conditions on which they shall be granted.
Do I understand the minister to say that the section in the Bill fixing the capital at $100,000 shall be construed by the department to mean that there must be assets over liabilities to that extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

months instead of fifteen. The minister cannot see each of these men personally, and I think it is a mistake to leave the Act in this slipshod manner. This is a matter which should not be left to the officials to decide, according to whether the applicant is friend or foe. The law provides for six months' residence duties in each homestead year. I am inclined to think that in the case I mentioned, where a man was in funds twenty months after the first instalment became due, the officials would make him put in two periods of six months each. If all these cases came before the minister personally, I have no doubt that he would do what was just, but it .is hardly necessary ifor me to repeat that there are men in his department upon whose justice I would not always rely; and I think he is making a mistake in not making that point clear.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The strict interpretation
would require what the hon. gentleman states, but we are not putting any more power in the hands of our officials than they now possess. There must be a certain amount of elasticity in the interpretation and enforcement of the law. The good sense of those charged with the administration of the Act will have to decide each case on its merits.
Will the minister say that the residence duties for a fraction of a year shall be not more than, in the ratio of six months to twelve months?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), Bill No. 120, to correct a clerical error in Act 1-2 George V, chapter 118, respecting the National Weekly Indemnity Company, and to change its name to the Merchants and Employers Guarantee and Accident Company, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section I-business of company:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MERCHANTS AND EMPLOYERS ACCIDENT GUARANTEE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The purpose of this Bill is merely to correct a translator's error in

the English version of the Act. The act sought to be amended was originally a private Bill presented in French, but, when it came to be translated, the word ' cautionnement ' was translated as * bond ' instead of ' guarantee.5 One of the purposes of the company was to do guarantee insurance but the translator rendered it as bond insurance. This Bill originally contained one section correcting that error but I may say that it will be necessary to put in another clause, because the same error occurred in another section of the Bill which was not noticed at the time the Bill was prepared. Furthermore, the Insurance Department having pointed out that the regulations they imposed in regard to the capital were imposed in view of the English version, it will 'be necessary to further amend the Bill to meet the requirements as to capital suitable for a company to do a guarantee insurance business. I therefore beg to move that the Bill as before the committee be amended by adding the following sections:
2.	Subsection 2 of section 8 of chapter 118 of the English version of the statutes of 1911 is amended by striking out the word ' bond ' in the second line thereof and inserting the word ' guarantee ' in lieu thereof.
3.	Subsection 2 of section 8 of chapter 118 in both the English and French versions of the statutes of 1911 is amended by striking out the words ' eighty thousand dollars ' in the fourth line thereof and inserting in lieu thereof the words ' one hundred and twenty thousand dollars, but the new company may commence the business of guarantee insurance in addition to accident insurance and sickness insurance when its paid-up capital stock amounts to ninety-five thousand dollars, or may commence the business of burglary insurance in addition to accident insurance and sickness insurance when its paid-up capital stock amounts to sixty-five thousand dollars.'
4.	Subsection 4 of section 8 of chapter 118 in both the English and French versions of the statutes of 1911 is amended by striking out the word ' thirty ' in the fourth line thereof and inserting the word ' seventy ' in lieu thereof.
The two last sections are introduced to meet the requirements of the Insurance Department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MERCHANTS AND EMPLOYERS ACCIDENT GUARANTEE COMPANY.
speechtext: Where is the head office of this company?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MERCHANTS AND EMPLOYERS ACCIDENT GUARANTEE COMPANY.
speechtext: In Montreal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MERCHANTS AND EMPLOYERS ACCIDENT GUARANTEE COMPANY.
speechtext: Where was it incorporated?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MERCHANTS AND EMPLOYERS ACCIDENT GUARANTEE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The company by another name was originally incorporated in the province of Quebec, and by a statute of 1911 the name was changed to the Merchants'
and Employers' Guarantee and Accident Company, and provisions were made with regard to the capital that would be required in order to the carrying on of the business. The reason these changes have to be made is, that in determining the amount that would be required with regard to capital at the time the Bill was passed, the Insurance Department acted upon the English version and required a capital suitable to the doing of a bond insurance business, which I understand is less than would be required for the doing of a guarantee business. The anomalous situation was created that whereas, under the French version of the statute which was based upon the petition whicn was in French, the company was authorized to do this guarantee business, under the English version it was apparently only authorized to do a bond insurance business. The requirement as regards capital was based upon the English version and, therefore, only provided for a capital such as, in the opinion of the department, was necessary to justify the carrying on of a bond insurance business. It comes as a public Bill because it has been represented that the mistake which called for correction was the mistake of the officers of the House. The petitioners put their petition before the House in a language which they were entitled to use, and in the French version it was perfectly clear that a guarantee business was sought, but an error occurred in the translation and it was carried through and not noticed until later. The Insurance Department has recommended that these other changes which are consequent on that original error should be made.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) moved that the House go into 'Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that It is expedient to provide for three additional members of the Senate for the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It might be
well to discuss this matter now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The province of British Columbia was brought into Confederation by an Order in Council which provided that it should be represented in the Senate of Canada by three members. A close consideration of the statutes under which that

Order in Council was passed might lead to the conclusion that possibly something had been overlooked. However, the Order in Council has been acted upon for a great .many years, and British Columbia has always been regarded as being represented in the Senate by three members, and it is so represented to-day. When the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were created in 1905, provision was made that they should each be represented by four members and after the next decennial ceu-sus that the number might be increased to six. When the addition was made to the territory of Manitoba in 1911 a similar provision was made in regard to that province, namely, that its representation in the Senate, which at that time consisted of four, should after the next decennial census be increased to six. The original basis of representation in the various provinces in the Senate was not fixed by population, nor does it seem to have been fixed upon any principle that could very well be defined. The representation as fixed seems to have been purely arbitrary. There was a provision that the provinces then constituting Confederation should be divided into three divisions: Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime provinces. It was provided that Ontario should be represented in the Senate of Canada by twenty-four members, that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick should each be represented in the Senate b>
twelve members, and that Quebec should be represented by twenty-four members, it being provided that in the province of Quebec the representation should be assigned to certain divisions in that prov ince, whereas in the other provinces of Canada the representation is at large. It was provided that in case the province of Prince Edward Island should be admitted to Confederation, the representation of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick should be reduced by four, and that Prince Edward Island should be assigned a representation of four in the Senate. Provision was also made for the representation of Newfoundland in the Senate should that colony be admitted to Confederation. There was also the provision that His Majesty the King, by Order in Council, might increase the representation in the Senate by either three or six. In case of an increase by the number of three, one should be taken from Ontario, one from Quebec and one from the Maritime provinces. If the representation should he increased

by six, two should be taken from Ontario, two from Quebec and two from the Maritime provinces, and no new senators should be appointe'd from either of these provinces until after the number fixed by the British North America Act should be reduced below the number which I have mentioned, that is, twenty-four for each division. There has been no provision for the constitution or establishment of a fourth senatorial division in Canada, beyond the provision to which I have just now alluded; and the proposal to increase the representation of the four western provinces to the number of six each would bring about in effect the establishment of a fourth division, although, so far as those provisions in the British North America Act which provide for a temporary increase in certain cases are concerned, it would be necessary to have an amendment to the British North America Act for the purpose of establishing proper provisions in that regard. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition alluded to this matter when one of these Bills was under discussion some time ago; and, if I remember his words correctly, he suggested that it would be a very proper thing to establish a fourth division for representation in the Senate of Canada consisting of the four provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. The proposals which we have laid before the House in that regard will carry out his suggestion except as regards the necessity of some amendment to the British North America Act to which I have alluded. I think it is clear that any legislation passed by this Parliament for the purpose of increasing the representation of the province of British Columbia in the Senate would have to be confirmed by British legislation. As far as that is concerned, we would not propose to bring the legislation into effect until such confirmatory legislation should have been obtained. There is a precedent for the course which I am proposing to follow in this regard in the legislation passed for rihe purpose of appointing a deputy Speaker in the Senate in 1894. This legislation was passed with the proviso that it should not come into' force until His Majesty's pleasure was signified by proclamation in the Canada Gazette. The question as to whether or not Parliament had the power to pass that legislation was submitted to the law officers of the Crown in Great Britain; and, although they doubted whether any confirmatory legislation was

necessary, such confirmatory legislation was passed in 1895. It is desirable, I think, that the province of British Columbia should be placed upon the same basis as the other western provinces in respect of its representation in the Senate, and I think I have already placed upon the table of the House a resolution of the legislature of that province passed during a recent session. It was transmitted to the Government by the following communication :
Province of British Columbia.
The 3rd of March, 1914.
At Government House,
Victoria, B.C.
Sir,-I have the honour to forward herewith, a copy of an approved minute embodying- a resolution of the Legislative Assembly of this province, in which application is made to the federal Government for an increase in the number of senators representing the province.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Thos. W. Paterson, Lieutenant Governor.
The Honourable
The Secretary of State,
Ottawa.
The resolution alluded to is as follows:
The Committee of Council submit for the approval of His Honour the Lieutenant Governor a resolution of the Legislative Assembly of the province of British Columbia, as follows :
Whereas the Parliament of Canada has under consideration a measure providing for the redistribution of the constituencies of the Dominion :
And whereas it is provided to make provision for the appointment of an additional number of senators:
And whereas it is provided that the number of senators for each of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta shall be six:
And whereas the population of British Columbia, as ascertained by the census in 1911, compares favourably with the other provinces mentioned and is increasing rapidly:
And whereas the area and importance of the province of British Columbia make it necessary and advisable that this province should receive' adequate recognition when such appointments are made:
Therefore, be it resolved that His Honour the Lieutenant-Governor be requested to forward through the proper channels to the Dominion Government the prayer of this House that the number of senators for the province of British Columbia be increased to six, so as to give British Columbia equal standing in the Upper House with the other western provinces. .
The committee advise that a copy of this minute be transmitted to the Honourable the Secretary of State of Canada.
Henry Esson Young,
Clerk, Executive Council.
Victoria, 2nd March, 1914.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There are before the House at the present time four
resolutions to increase the representation in the Senate of the four western provinces, namely, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, in order to give each of these provinces six members instead of what they have at present. As to the desirability of such legislation, for my part, I have no objection to offer. On the contrary, some years ago, at the time we created the two new provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, I pointed out that it would be advisable that we should do for the western provinces what had been done for the eastern provinces, namely, create a new division, which would be called the western division, and which would make the number of divisions four. As stated by my right hon. friend a moment ago, when Confederation was established three divisions were created for the purpose of senatorial representation, that is to say, Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime provinces, each of which three divisions was given twenty-four members. The fathers of Confederation foresaw that, as time went on, new provinces would be added to Confederation, and they made provision for representation in the Senate of two provinces, namely, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, which it was supposed would come into Confederation. The dispositions which they made with regard to Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland were just as has been stated by my right hon. friend. With regard to Prince Edward Island, it was stated that, when it came into Confederation, it would be entitled to four members, but that these four members would be deducted from the twenty-four members from the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, leaving twenty-four as the unit of representation for the division consisting of the Maritime provinces. At the same time it was stated that Newfoundland would be given a representation of four, making the total number of senators seventy-six instead of seventy-two. Strange to say, although the fathers of Confederation foresaw that British Columbia might come into Confederation, no disposition was- made as to its representation in the Senate. When British Columbia came into Confederation, it was given representation in the Senate of three members, thus adding three to the total membership of the Senate, which had been fixed by the British North America Act at seventy-two. The matter evidently was an oversight at the time; but still, as stated by my right hon. friend, more than forty years have elapsed since that date, and, although British Columbia has been represented in the Senate perhaps without

authority, it would be to no purpose to question what has been done. I have only this, however, to observe to my right hon. friend, that in so far as two of the provinces, namely, Alberta and Saskatchewan, are concerned, whose membership in the Senate it is now sought to increase, there is no constitutional objection; we have the power in this Parliament to give them this increased representation. So far as British Columbia is concerned, nay right hon. friend can see that we have no power, but that anything we do must be confirmed by the Imperial Parliament. I submit, with all due deference, that so far as Manitoba also is concerned, we have no power at present to increase the representation of that province in the Senate than we have in the case of British Columbia. It is true, that two years ago when we extended the boundaries of Manitoba, we introduced into the Bill a provision to the effect that Manitoba should be represented in the Senate by six; but I submit with great confidence to the judgment of my right hon. friend that this was simply an expression of our will that the thing should be done by the proper authorities, and that the Parliament of Canada as now constituted has no power to increase the representation of Manitoba in the Senate. I would submit to my right hon. friend the advisability of proceeding in a different way from that which he now proposes. I think undoubtedly we have no power to increase the representation of British Columbia in the Senate; and in my opinion-I do not know whether that opinion is shared by hon. members on the other side-we have no such power in relation to Manitoba, or that at best our power to increase the representation in Manitoba would not be held to be above doubt. Therefore, I submit to my right hon. friend that it would be better to proceed as we have proceeded in such circumstances before when we were asking for imperial legislation and, instead of passing Acts which we have not the power to pass and then asking confirmation by the imperial authorities, to proceed by way of Royal Address asked by the Senate and the House of Commons to His Majesty asking for the necessary legislation, which would give us the powers we have not now. I repeat what I said a moment ago, that in view of the development that is taking place in the provinces of the West they are certainly entitled to increased representation in the Senate, and as a group I think the representation should be increased to twenty-four. I think it would be more in [Sir Wilfrid I.aurier 1
accordance with the constitutional usage if we passed an Address declaring that we create a new group composed of the western provinces to be given representation of twenty-four-a new group of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, just as we have the group of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island-and that its representation in the Senate be twenty-four members.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The observations of my
right hon. friend, are, of course, entitled to very careful consideration. Perhaps this resolution might be permitted to pass at present, so that the Bill may be introduced and I will confer with my right hon. friend before taking any further action in regard to it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. BORDEN thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 184, respecting the representation of the province of British Columbia in the Senate.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) the House went into Committee on Bill No. 174, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act amendment, 1908, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-appointment of deputy judge:

What is the object of
this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose is to empower the judge of the Juvenile Delinquents Court to appoint a deputy judge, the appointment to be made subject to the approval of the Attorney General of the province. It has been found in some of the large centres, and I may say particularly in the city of Montreal, that there are occasions when it is impossible for the judge to be in attendance day by day and do the work. At present in the absence of the judge, they have to call in a police magistrate. While these gentleman who are called in, no doubt, do their work very effectively, still it has been considered undesirable that a person not accustomed to the administration of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which, as the hon. gentleman

knows, looks rather to paternal correction than to the administration of criminal justice, should intervene in the operation of the court.
It seems desirable that some one accustomed to the system should be appointed to do the routine work. I think it is probable that in many instajnoes clerical officers of the court will be appointed deputy judges. This legislation has been strongly urged by Judge Choquet, whom everybody will recognize as being what may be called an expert in the administration of this particular law. It has been suggested, however, that there may be cases where it may not he considered desirable by persons interested in some of these juvenile delinquents that the matter should be dealt with otherwise than by the judge himself. To meet that view, I move that the Act be amended by adding a second section, providing that:
No deputy judge shall hear and determine any case which a Juvenile Court committee desires should be reserved for hearing and determination by the judge of the Juvenile Court.
The Act provides for the constitution of a committee of citizens, acting gratuitously, to co-operate with the judge of the Juvenile Court and I know that in Montreal there are very active committees of that kind which take a live interest in the treatment of the children who are brought before these courts. It has been- thought that, when in their judgment any case is deemed to be of such a nature that the judge himself should deal with it, they should have the right to make a request to that effect, and that that request should be granted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I quite approve of this legislation. From what I can gather, the Juvenile Court in the city of Montreal has, under the -able direction of Mr. Justice Ghoquet, been a great success. There is, however, an amendment which I would suggest to my hon. Mend and in doing so I simply voice the opinion expressed by many friends of the Juvenile Court. It i3 that the proceedings of the court should be kept more private; that is to say, that they should not -be made public through the -press. Several organizations and religious bodies im Montreal have made representations to the Attorney General to this end. The Juvenile -Court was created by Parliament because it was thought that young boys and young girls who fall in early life 22SJ
-should be kept away from the older criminals and given a chance of reforming themselves through their receiving paternal treatment on the part of society, represented by the judge. On several occasions I have noticed that cases coming before the juvenile court were fully reported in the press. I am a friend of the press and a -sort of journalist myself, but I think that -quite .enough news of this kind may be obtained from the other courts without the proceedings of the juvenile courts being published.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
I am aware of this, but, unfortunately, I can point to some instances where the reports were published, much -against the view of those who take an interest in these courts.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
At one o'clock the House took reces-s.
The House resumed at Three o'clock.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
That it is expedient to provide that there may be paid and applied from and out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, a sum not exceeding in the whole one million two hundred thousand dollars to pay to persons who were creditors for money on deposit in the Farmers Bank of Canada, the respective amounts standing at their credit in the books of the bank when the bank suspended payment.

Is there any understanding in regard to this Bill? I do not know



what the intention of the leader of the Opposition is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that* following the usual course, the principal discussion will take place upon the second reading. In the meantime, I shall be very glad to explain in a general way, if any gentleman desires it, the reasons for the Government's proposals.

Perhaps the minister might give a brief explanation.
Mr. WHITE': My hon. friend from Halifax having asked me to explain, I may say that the proposals of the Government embodied in this resolution are founded upon the report of Sir William Meredith, now Chief Justice of Ontario, who, it may be recalled, was in 1912 appointed a commissioner to investigate the affairs of the Farmers Bank of Canada from its incorporation. His report, we submit, establishes that the certificate of the Treasury Board, which, under the Bank Act, was necessary before the bank could open for business, was obtained by false and fraudulent representations. In this connection, I might call attention to the first paragraph of page 8 of the printed report of the commissioner, which reads as follows:
My conclusion on this branch of the inquiry is that the Treasury Board was induced to give its certificate by false and fraudulent representations on the part of Travers, and that if the facts I have mentioned as to the way in which the $250,000 was made up had been disclosed, the certificate of the Treasury Board would not have been given.
I might also draw attention to section 3 of page 9 of the report, which reads as follows:
It is true that, as Mr. Fielding stated in evidence, Travers, so far as he knew, was a reputable banker; but that was not, in my opinion, a sufficient reason for not having instituted an inquiry as to the matters which had been called to his attention. Such an inquiry could easily have been made, and the delay occasioned by it would have been inconsiderable, and such an inquiry would, undoubtedly, have resulted in the discovery of the manner in which the $100,000 had been raised and in the refusal of the Treasury Board to give the certificate.
The report of the commissioner further establishes negligence on the part of the Treasury Board in the issue of the certificate. Paragraph 6 of page 8 of the printed report of the commissioner is as follows:
I do not suggest that the minister would have been justified because of the information
[Mr. Oliver. J
conveyed to him in recommending that the certificate should not be granted, or that the Treasury Board because of it would not have been -justified in refusing to grant it, but, having received the information, it was in my opinion incumbent on the Treasury Board to have investigated the charges that had been made before coming to a conclusion as to whether or not the certificate should be given.
Briefly, the inquiry referred to in this paragraph would have shown that Travers, the general manager, and wrecker of the bank, had made a false declaration to the Minister of Finance and to the Treasury Board. It would have shown that the provisional directors had made a five years' contract with Travers, and put him in control of the organization and business of the bank. I would call attention, in passing, to paragraph 3 on page 5 of the report:
It appears clear from these agreements and resolutions that what was intended was to sell the charter of the bank to Travers and to put him in control of its organization and business, and that the provisional directors should abdicate their functions and act in accordance with his directions, and that is what followed.
If the certificates had not been granted the bank would not have commenced business; or if, afterwards, the provisions of the Bank Act had been strictly complied with the bank would not have started business with Travers as its general manager, because if the Treasury Board had made the inquiry which the commissioner finds it was incumbent upon them to have made, the character of Travers would have been disclosed. Of course, if the bank had not started business, or if, starting business it had been under prudent and honest management, the loss which followed would not have ensued to the depositors.
After all, is not the finding of the commissioner that if the bank had not started there would not have been any loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think the commissioner explicitly finds that. I am arguing that if the certificate of the Treasury Board had not been given the bank could not have opened its doors for business.
And thereby there would not have been any loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Therefore, there could not have been any loss. If, on the other hand, at a later date, the provisions of the statute had been complied with, if $500,000 of bona fide subscriptions had been received, and $250,000 in cash paid thereon, as required

by the Bank Act then, assuming this inquiry had been made it would have been impossible for Travers to have been placed at the head of the bank, because the inquiry, which the commissioner finds it was incumbent on the Treasury Board to have made, would have disclosed that Travers had perjured himself in the statutory declaration which he made to the Minister of Finance. But, by reason of the negligence of the Treasury Board, as established by the commissioner, the bank was allowed to start on its ill-fated career, and with Travers as general manager at its head.- Travers, whom the Treasury Board would *have discovered, if they had made the necessary inquiry, a man who had perjured himself in his declaration, and was wholly undependable and unreliable. That, in a general way, is the argument in favour of the Government proposal in this matter. speechtext: The proceeds of the option on the Keeley mine, as I explained, are included in this statement of assets and: with that included there will be nothing *left for the depositors on savings and current accounts. In the Bill which I propose-to introduce, the Government upon payment of the depositors, will be subrogated to their rights in the liquidation. In the event of there being any balance, that would belong to the Government and the Government would be entitled to the benefits of the shb~ rogation.

Will the parties who
nave money on credit with the bank, though without having it actually on deposit, get .any benefit from this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Bill covers only depositors on current and saving accounts; it does not cover those who hold drafts ox money orders on the bank.
222i

I noticed in the press a statement to the effect that there was some agreement existing between the depositors and the shareholders as to the partition of any amount received from the Government under this 'Bill. Will the minister inform the House if he knows of any such payment, and if so, what is the nature of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no authentic information respecting the agreement in question. I have seen in the press, no doubt the same reports that my hon. friend has seen, in which it has been stated that depositors, of their own motion, would contribute such an amount from the sums which were received from the Government as would relieve the shareholders from their double liability, but I have no official knowledge of it nor do I know whether all the depositors, or, if some, how many, have entered into such an agreement. My information is hearsay only, as, I understand, is the case with my hon. friend.

The minister stated that the Government would be subrogated in their rights; will the Government exact the double liability from the shareholders?
Mr .WHITE .The G-overnment would not be in a position to exact anything. The liquidation is under the Dominion Winding-up Act, and it would be the duty of the liquidator to carry out his liquidation under the provisions of that Act. That would include the question of double liability. After all the liabilities are paid and the costs and expenses of the liquidation provided for, in the event of there being a surplus which would be available for the depositors on current and savings account, the Government would be subrogated to their rights in respect of such surplus available for them. But I must state to my hon. friend that the question is not likely to arise, for the reason that the liquidator has included in this statement, which I have placed upon ' Hansard,' the sum of $120,779 as the estimated value of the uncollected portion of the double liability, and even with that amount included the assets would appear to me, on the statement insufficient to meet the liabilities other than those to depositors. So that, in so far as the subrogation clause _ is concerned, I do not suggest that the Government will receive anything in respect to it, so far as I can judge from the statement which has been furnished me by the liquidator.

In concluding my remarks, which have 'been general in character, and reserving what I have to say in greater detail to the second reading of the Bill, I desire to call attention to the remarks of the commissioner on page 10 of the printed report as to the conduct of the bank under Travers and the nature of the failure of the bank. He says:
The subsequent management of the affairs of the hank was characterized by gross extravagance, recklessness, incompetency, dishonesty and fraud, and has resulted in the entire loss of the paid-up capital and the whole of the deposits, and that after allowing for all that can be extracted from the shareholders on their double liability a loss amounting to no less than $1,806,437, making a record unparalleled in the history of any bank in Canada, or, as far as I am aware, in any other country.
For the present, that is all I desire to say with regard to the resolution.

Does the minister intend to safeguard the depositors irrespective of the shareholders? It is known to a great many members of this House that copies of an agreement have been sent, I presume to all of the shareholders, asking that they sign them. This agreement provides in the main that if the depositors receive their deposits they will pay thirty per cent, of them for the benefit of the shareholders, so that there may be no double liability upon th& shareholders. I do not know that any one in the constituency I represent is interested particularly in the matter, but I have several clients from adjoining counties who have consulted me on that point, and I know from others that copies of this agreement have been sent them, and also letters, threatening them that if they do not sign they will not get anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I ask merely for information; is my hon. friend aware as to how far these agreements have been signed, 'because I am not?

No, but I know from
some hon. members in this House that they have advised the depositors to sign, and I would like to know if it is the intention of the minister or of the Government to safeguard the depositors, even those who have signed these special agreements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How do you mean to safeguard them?

To see that the money is actually paid to the depositors, and we can do that by inserting a clause rendering

null and void any agreements that have been heretofore signed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Government's action in this matter is not dependent in any degree whatever on what depositors may or may not do with their money. As I stated to my hon. friend from Halifax, I have no knowledge, except of a hearsay character, as to the agreement or agreements which have been referred to. If the depositor receives payment from the Government of Canada, I suppose it will be his money to deal with as he sees fit. It is the intention that these cheques shall be sent to the depositors themselves, from the Finance Department, when this Bill becomes law. Further than that, I do not see how it is possible to fetter the action of the depositors when they receive the money. My hon. friend has suggested that a clause might be inserted in the Bill that would safeguard the depositors, but if the depositor desires to use his money in a certain way after he receives it, I do not see how we can restrict him in what would appear to me to be his undoubted right. A question would also arise as to any agreements which he may have signed- and I have no knowledge as to how many of such agreements have been signed-as the question of how far a person has bound himself by contract would appear to me to be concerned with property and civil rights, unless, of course, it came exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Dominion Parliament and we were dealing with it by legislation. If we discuss that here we will get into pretty deep legal waters.
If the cheque is sent to the individual depositor and not to any representative of the depositors, I think that will pretty well safeguard it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My idea is to send it direct.

The legislation which the Government purposes founding upon the resolution we are now considering is, I think, very regrettable indeed, and is establishing an extremely bad precedent. Further, I believe this legislation is proposed in face of the pretty strongly and generally expressed opposition of the people of this country. However, as the minister has suggested that it is more fitting that the discussion in detail upon the proposed Bill be postponed until the second reading, I .agree in that. I would like to ask the minister a question or two in respect to some returns I asked for the other day.
In the first place, I asked for a return giving the names of the depositors with the amounts of their deposits. I understand that the return has been placed upon the table of the House, but I believe it is very voluminous. My reason for requesting that return was that I wanted to ascertain what was the average amount deposited by each depositor. I would like to inquire if it is possible for the minister to direct that a statement be prepared by his officials between now and the second reading of the Bill, showing the number of depositors with, amounts between one dollar and $1,000, and between $1,000 and $2,000, and so on, deposited by each.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I can give the hon. gentleman that information now.

I would be glad if the hon. minister would put it on ' Hansard.' I want also to call, the minister's attention to the fact that I asked (for a return showing the amount of deposits at the end of each year beginning with 1906, the year of incorporation, and ending with 1910, the year the bank was suspended. If my hon. friend could give me that information now and place it upon ' Hansard,' I would be much obliged. Further, when the minister rises, I would like him to explain upon what principle the Government has decided to decline to meet the petition of the shareholders, and upon what principle he differentiates between the claims made -by the shareholders and the claims made by the depositors.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Answering my hon. friend in. detail, I laid upon the table, I think in his absence, the other day, a list of all the depositors of the Farmers Bank, upon both current and savings accounts. I have also laid upon the table the return to which he has referred showing the amount of deposits on current and on savings accounts as of the close of the years, 1907, 1908, 1909 and 1910. My hon. friend has not seen that return, but it was laid upon the table within the last two or three days.

Has my hon. friend laid
upon the table a list of the shareholders; if not, will he do that also?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not been asked for that, and I have not such a list. I think, however, I can obtain it and lay it upon the table later on. My hon. friend from Halifax has desired to obtain some infor-
Does the memorandum proceed any further than my hon. friend has read?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. If my hon. friend
would like to have the number of depositors havings deposits 'between the several thousands I cam get that information, if he thinks it is essential for the discussion of the Bill.
I would like to see it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will endeavour to get
the information.
Is my hon. friend going to allow the depositors any interest on their deposits?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think the depositors will insist upon interest.
The same principle will apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You are speaking of the interest, not the principal.
My hon. friend from Halifax has asked as to how we differentiate the shareholders from the depositors. I think that is an easy differentiation. The shareholders of the bank are the proprietors of the bank; they elect their directors; the directors select or continue in office the manager and other

officers having under their control the administration of the bank. We cannot see any principle upon which the Government is justified in affording relief to the shareholders, because, as I have said, the shareholders are the proprietors, the owners of the bank, carrying on its business subject to the provisions of the Bank Act. If their directors, or the agent or agents of their directors, are dishonest or, by incompetence, extravangance or fraud, dissipate the assets of the bank, the shareholders cannot be heard to say that they have any claim for relief. [DOT]

The other day I put on the Order Paper a question which was answered by my hon. friend, and which was as follows:
Does the Government intend to reimburse the depositors of La Banque Ville Marie, La Banque du Peuple, and La Banque de St. Jean, three banks that have failed during the last fifteen or sixteen years?
My hon. friend answered ' mo.' Since getting that answer I have received some letters. The county of Rou ville, which I represent, the county of St. Jean, and Iberville and in some degree the county of St. Hyacinthe have been very deeply mulcted by the failure of La Banque de St. Jean two years ago. Especially in the parishes of St. Cesaire, St. Paul, Marieville, Ste. Angfele and L'Ange Gardien; many of my electors, many widows and many minors have been practically ruined by the failure of that bank.
As regards La Banque Ville Marie, I know perhaps more intimately the cause of the failure, because at that time I was practising law in Montreal; and I, with Mr. Gxeenshields K. C., happened [to be retained as counsel to defend some of those who were arrested in connection with the failure of the bank. We all know that the president and the manager were sent to jail, and that many people were ruined as a consequence of the failure.
We also know the causes of the failure of La Banque du Peuple. The manager had to leave the country and died in Chicago, ruining a large number of people. La Banque du Peuple, after the bank of Montreal, is the oldest in Old Canada, and the oldest amongst the French-Canadian families had their fortunes more or less involved in that bank. My hon. friend will understand that I am .sincere in asking this explanation. The people who have been affected by the failure of these banks will hardly understand why there is a differential treatment in their case. I might tell

my hon. friend that the management of La Banique Ville Marie and La Banque de St. Jean, and perhaps in a less degree of La Banque du Peuple, was characterized by the same recklessness as is described in the report signed by Chief Justice Meredith. When I recall what took place after the failure of La Banque Ville Marie, and of what took place before the court subsequent to the failure of La Banque St. Jean, I say this language applies exactly to those cases:
The subsequent management of the affairs of the bank was characterized by gross extravagance, recklessness, incompetency, dishonesty and fraud, and has resulted in the entire loss of the paid-up capital and the [DOT] whole of the deposits.
I say this language applies exactly to the management of these other banks. And the people will not understand why different treatment is meted out to those who lost their money in these banks and those who lost their money in the Farmers' Bank. Now, my hon. friend should give an explanation to the country, to the unfortunate depositors and shareholders-or let me say depositors, for I understand that the shareholders are not to be reimbursed-he should give an explanation to the unfortunate depositors of these banks setting forth the reason why they are not treated in the same way as the depositors of the Farmers' Bank are treated. I ask that in all sincerity and all frankness, reserving any further criticism of the subject for the present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I observed that my hon. friend was not in his place during the earlier part of my remarks upon the resolution. I supplied then the reason for the Government's action in bringing in a measure to reimburse the depositors in the Farmers Bank. He has referred to the consequences of certain bank failures. We all agree that in this and in all other cases of bank failures, the results have been most tragic-I think that is the word he used-
' to those who have lost through the failure of these banks and by the incompetence, fraud, and dishonesty of those in charge of those banks' affairs. My hon. friend has fixed upon one part of the report of the commissioner, at page 10, which he quotes, and he says that these remarks of this commissioner would apply equally to all the banks which he has drawn to my attention. But I would point out to him that the Government is not taking this action because of the fact that the banks' administration was characterized by ' gross extravagance, recklessness, incompetency, dishonesty and fraud ', to use the words of the commissioner-*
The hon. gentleman himself quoted that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I quoted that passage to show the character of the administration of the bank, but I say that the Government's action is not on that ground, or rather not solely on that ground; but, as I pointed out at the outset of my remarks, is based upon the finding of the commissioner, now Chief Justice of Ontario, which, I submit, shows conclusively that the conditions prescribed by the Bank Act as precedent to the issuance of the certificate of the Treasury Board had not been complied with, that the certificate had been obtained by fraud and dishonesty, and that the Treasury Board had been negligent in issuing it. The basis of the Government's action is negligence on the part of the Treasury Board, and I will read for the benefit of my hon. friend the portion of the report that I read during my remarks at the beginning of this discussion. I read from the printed report of the commissioner, page 8, first paragraph:
My conclusion on this branch of the Inquiry is that the Treasury Board was induced to give its certificate by false and fraudulent representations on the part of Travers, and that if the facts I have mentioned as to the way in which tne $250,000 was made up had been disclosed, the certificate of the Treasury Board would not have been given.
I read paragraph 6 on the same page:
I do not suggest that the minister would have been justified because of the information conveyed to him in recommending that the certificate should not be granted, or that the Treasury Board because of it would not have been justified in refusing to grant it, but, having received the information

That is to say, in reference to the fraud which was being practised by Travers.
-it was in my opinion incumbent on the Treasury Board to have investigated the charges that had been made before coming to a conclusion as to whether or not the certificate should be given.
It was ' incumbent upon the Treasury Board.' That is it was the duty of the Treasury Board, which duty the Treasury Board did not fulfil. Now, breach of duty is negligence. Therefore, the basis of the Government's action is negligence on the part of the Treasury Board which issued the certificate after express notice received that there had been irregularity. If the Treasury Board had made the inquiry which the commissioner says it was incumbent upon them to make, the bank would never have opened its doors for business, or if the

irregularities had been cured subsequently, the bank would never have opened its doors for business with Travers as general manager, because the inquiry which the commissioner says it was incumbent upon the Treasury Board to make would have disclosed the fact that Travers was a perjurer and a wholly unreliable person. And I pointed out that Travers had a five years' contract with the directors of the bank. The result was that the bank was launched- the provisions of the Bank Act not having been complied with-with Travers at its head and with consequent loss to the depositors. Now, my hon. friend says:	How do you
differentiate this ease from the case of the other banks? It is not the policy of the Government, I repeat-it has never been the policy of any government in Canada-to reimburse depositors or other creditors of banks that have failed. Where I differentiate this case from the cases that have been drawn to my attention and all other cases is this,-that this Treasury certificate should not have been granted. That certificate was granted by the Treasury Board, and the Government is responsible for the action of the Treasury Board, at least morally; and the Treasury Board's action in this case was negligent, according to the findings of the commissioner. The hon. member for Rouville says that the people will not understand. But in view of the explanation I make, the people will understand. And I am aware that, now that I have made the explanation, he will help me to get the people to understand. If he will reply to the parties who have written to him, or if when he is upon the platform as he frequently is in dealing with political matters, he will say, that the Government's action in this case does not form a precedent, because in no other case has there been established negligence in the issue of the certificate, the people will understand and no misunderstanding will arise as to the action of the Government.
I repeat^although it would seem to me to be an unnecessary repetition-that the principle of the Government's granting relief in this case is the negligence of the Treasury Board, and the loss which resulted to the depositors of the Farmers' Bank as a natural consequence and outcome of that negligence.
May I ask the minister if this sum is to be paid in lieu of damages?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No one has contended
that these depositors have a legal right against the Government which they could 
enforce by action. The Government's course is not based upon its legal liabilities, although I think on legal principles the Government is bound to reimburse these depositors. I think it can hardly be said, therefore, that payment by the Government is compensation for damages sustained by the depositors.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is not the occasion upon which to discuss the principles involved in this Bill; that discussion will come more properly on the second reading. But without waiting for that occasion, I must at once protest against the imputation-not only the imputation, but the charge-made by my hon. friend against Mr. Fielding: that he was guilty of negligence in issuing the certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I made it against the Treasury Board, on the finding of the commissioner.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Treasury Board was presided over by the Minister of Finance of the day; therefore the expression of my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance, no matter in what language it may be clothed, implies-not only implies, but asserts-that his predecessor in office was negligent of the duties incumbent upon him. I protest against the language of the Minister of Finance and say that he has no reason for making such a grave assertion against, a man of Mr. Fielding's character. I call the attention of the committee and of my hon. friend especially to the language of Mr. Justice Meredith, page 9 of the report:
There is, in my opinion, no ground for supposing that any improper influence was used to induce the Treasury Board to give the certificate or to induce the Minister of Finance to recommend the granting of it, and the most that can properly be charged against the Department of Finance or the Treasury Board is an error of judgment.
Error of judgment and negligence are two different things. Error of judgment cannot be called negligence of duty; it is an error in itself. But when you imply negligence, you imply that the party alleged to be guilty of that negligence did something which should not have been done and could not have been done without violating the moral law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no, not the moral law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I say that a man who is guilty of negligence has violated the moral law, and a violation of the


moral law is, in my opinion, a fault, if not a crime. But nothing of the kind can be charged against Mr. Fielding. The judge's finding upon this matter is that Mr. Fielding would have been better advised if he had prosecuted his inquiry more than he did; that is all. Therefore the imputation which my hon. friend wishes to make does not apply in this case. If there was negligence on the part of Mr. Fielding the question of how far the Government would be responsible would be a very different question; the Government would be responsible morally, if not otherwise. If a minister of the Crown has made an error of judgment, it is simply a question of his having made a mistake which has no legal or moral consequences. Of course, there may have been political consequences. It is always a serious charge that there has been an error of judgment, but we are all liable to err, and, after all, if. the only charge that can be made against a minister of the Crown who has been fifteen years in office is that upon a certain occasion >he committed an error of judgment, the charge is but a minor one. As I have said, this present occasion is not the time to discuss the Bill, but I say it is not fair to Mr. Fielding to say that he has been guilty of negligence. The charge against him . is one of error in judgment; let that pass until we come to the second reading of the Bill.
With regard to the matter which has been brought up by the hon. member for South Wellington-the assignment of claims on the part of depositors-the hon. Minister of Finance said that the money was to be paid to the depositors and that what they should do with their own money was their own business, not his. I agree with that, but at the same time there is another aspect of this case which must receive consideration. I have myself received a letter from an elderly lady telling me that she was almost forced to make an assignment of her claim to the shareholders. While the minister has nothing to do with that, as I do not think it can be provided against in the Bill, I think it would be well that it should be understood that no assignment of claim, whether partial or total, will be encouraged by the department, but that cheques shall be issued to the depositors. No assignment of claim should be admitted; if that is understood I shall be satisfied.
I have a question to ask my hon. friend with regard to the Keeley mine.
4 p.m. Travers assigned that mine property which is alleged to be
of the value of $150,000. Mining property is of a very unstable character; its value may be very high to-day and very low tomorrow. Upon what basis is the optional price put at $150,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no information. except the statement of the liquidator that an option for $150,000 has been, given; that it is to be exercised within the next two months and that it is his view that it will probably be exercised.
I desire to take exception to the assertion of my right hon. friend that I have imputed, by using the term negligence, moral culpability to my predecessor in office. I call the committee to witness that I have upon every occasion dealt as fairly and justly as I believe it is possible fox a man to deal with my predecessor and his course in this House-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because he is not here to defend himself. I always bear in mind the saying of Lord Bacon, that you should be tender to the memory of your predecessor because some day you may be a predecessor yourself. It may be that as to the question of negligence there is a distinction between the French law and the English law, but I may point out to my hon. friend-and there is not an English lawyer in the House who will not support me in the opinion which I now express- that an error of judgment may constitute negligence and that negligence does not necessarily imply moral culpability of any kind or nature whatsoever. For example, at common law a man may be negligent who miscalculates distance upon the street in driving his conveyance, if an accident results, causing damage. A man is bound to exercise the care which an ordinary man would exercise in his conduct towards his fellowmen. A man, by mere error of judgment involving no suggestion of moral obliquity, may become responsible at common law for negligence and its consequences. I did not mention, except in so far as I read it from the report of the commissioner, the name of my predecessor, but, of course, I am advancing to the committee the reasons for this legislation and I must advance them as they exist. The reasons for this legislation are that, according to the finding of Sir William Meredith, the commissioner, the Treasury Board did not do what he says it was incumbent upon the Treasury Board to have done. I lay it down as a principle of law which cannot be

controverted that if it is incumbent upon an individual or public body to do something and that individual or public body does not discharge that duty which it is incumbent upon him or them to discharge, that constitutes negligence. I have stated that no legal rights accrue to the depositors against the Government, but I was seeking to justify-and I think I have justified-the action of the Government on the analogy of legal principle, and, therefore, it was perfectly proper for me-and I do not think my course can be animadverted upon at all-to establish, from the finding of the commissioner, that the Treasury Board had been negligent in the issue of the certificate. I have said, and I repeat, that that does not by any means mean that my predecessor in office was guilty of any moral lapse or obliquity in the discharge of his duties as chairman of that board. My hon, friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has quoted a paragraph from the report. I may say that the commissioner is. there dealing with the question of whether money had been used by Travers to procure the issue of the certificate. It had been suggested that there was some impropriety connected with the issue of the certificate; that Travers had used money to purchase, so to speak, the certificate, and it was in dealing with that aspect of the case that the commissioner made the remarks my hon. friend has quoted. The commissioner says:
There Is, in my opinion, no ground for supposing that any improper influence was used to induce the Treasury Board to give the certificate-
I have not for a moment suggested that there was.
-or to induce the Minister of Finance to recommend the granting of it,-
I have never suggested that it was so used.
-and the most that can properly be charged against the Department of Finance or the Treasury Board is an error of judgment.
I submit that that error of judgment under the circumstances was negligence, or what we call negligence at the English common law-failure, either through lack of judgment or otherwise, to discharge the duty which the commissioner finds it was incumbent upon them to discharge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are you going to proceed legally on this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, because, as I have said, the negligence cannot be established 
as against the Crown, or as against a minister of the Crown acting in his capacity as minister. What I have sought to do is to show that on legal analogy the action of the Government is justifiable by reason of the fact that the negligence to which I have referred on the part of the Treasury Board was the primary and original cause of the loss of this money to the depositors.
Do you say that was the finding of the commissioner? Because he finds to the contrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course, we knew before this report was issued that it was fraud on the part of Travers, and the recklessness and extravagance of his management, that brought this loss to the depositors of the bank; but my argument is this: if the 'Treasury Board had done what they should have done-in other words if they had not been negligent-then the character of Travers would have been discovered, the certificate would not have been issued, the bank would not have started, and there would have been no loss to the depositors.

If a man was
never born he would never sin.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No certificate, no bank and no Travers; no bank or no Travers, no loss to depositors. That is the chain.
I think the commissioner meant to ridicule that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think he made
any attempt to ridicule that position. The commissioner says in the concluding portion of his report:
Notwithstanding the irregularities on the part of Travers and his misconduct in connection with the application for the certificate, which I have mentioned, the evidence satisfies me that if the bank had been prudently and honestly managed there is no reason why it should not have succeeded.
Why blame Mr. Fielding?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree with that. It is
perfectly obvious that if the 'bank had been honestly managed there would have been no loss.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only say in answer to my hon. friend that I do not know of any political obligation that the Government has to discharge, and it might be that my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mr. Boss) could answer that question better than I can. I have given the grounds for the Government's action and, I think, strong and cogent reasons justifying this measure of relief to the depositors.

As far as I am personally
concerned, I have no political obligations to discharge in 'connection with the Farmers Bank, and in that regard I am probably in a more enviable position than the minister's colleagues. It seems to me that either the minister's argument goes too far, or that his Bill is not going far enough. If, as he says, the reason for this relief being given is that there was negligence on the part of the Finance Minister and the Treasury Board in the initial stages, that negligence caused loss to the shareholders as well as to the depositors, and if the basis is as he says, he should go further and help the shareholders as well as the depositors. Either his reasoning is not good, or his assistance to those who lost in the Farmers Bank does not go far enough. I think that what the hon. member for Halifax has suggested is probably correct, that the Government by this expenditure of $1,200,000 is trying to discharge some political obligations with which they have encumbered themselves. I do not believe that the Finance Minister, in his heart, believes that this is a good principle to establish. Speaking for myself, I think this is an exceptional case, and I do not think it should be allowed to become a precedent in connection with the banking affairs of this country.
