I may say plainly to the House that considering the greatness of the disaster in Ontario through the failure of the Farmers Bank I, personally, am in favour of repaying the depositors for two reasons, and probably more: firstly, because the injury to the farmers of this country is so widespread and deeply, felt; and secondly, because as a matter of principle-I know the minister does not agree with me in this-the depositors of every chartered bank in this country should be protected. I think the Government should compel the banks themselves to give this protection, and because they have' not done so is sufficient reason for' the minister assisting the Farmers Bank depositors at any rate. But I think the Government should go farther, and if the minister's argument is good, and in some way assist the shareholders also. If the minister did that-as has been agreed upon between the depositors and shareholders- it would be perfectly right so far as I can see, in this very exceptional case, which however, by proper legislation being enacted as I advocated last session should not be allowed to become nor could it become a precedent.
We had no branch of the Farmers Bank in my riding but some of the depositors did live in that riding, and I know depositors and shareholders who have suffered. They were both misled by the same fraud, misrepresentation and dishonesty. When the minister puts his proposed assistance upon the ground that he has, it is the duty of the Government to go farther than they have done or put their assistance upon some other ground.
Mr. LEMIEI7X:	In view of what has
been said by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White), would he not consider an application on behalf of the depositors of La Banque Ville Marie, La Banque du Peuple and La Banque St. Jean? I think that when my hon. friend is made aware of the facts in connection with the failure of these banks he will find that representations were made to the officers of the Finance Department at the time that the aforesaid banks were mismanaged. The people have it in their heads that if the officers of the Finance Department had been more diligent perhaps the failures might have been averted. I would like to have an answer from my hon. friend whether in view of this [DOT] legislation, in view of the fact that the Farmers Bank depositors are compensated, he will consider my application. Some yeaTS ago the then hon. member for Jacques Cartier, Mr. Monk, -and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) will remember, it-took very strong ground in this House that the depositors in La Banque du Peuple should be recouped their losses. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance says that this legislation is based on the fact that an error of judgment was committed by the Treasury Board. I have always been educated under

the British constitutional system to the notion that the King could do no wrong. Can we not compare the action taken by my hon. friend in so far as the Treasury Board is concerned with the action which might be taken by the Minister of Justice, for instance in a case of miscarriage of justice? My hon. friend contends that he does not recoup the depositors of the Farmers Bank because of the crookedness, extravagance or perversity of Travers and his associates but because forsooth, an error of judgment was committed by the Treasury Board. Now, Sir, is not the Government also responsible for the administration of justice? The appointment of judges is made by the Minister of Justice after a recommendation is brought before Council. You appoint a judge, say in my district; he is supposed to be well versed in the law, honest and sober. He goes on the Bench, a case is brought before him, and, as a result of his inebriety, or his dishonesty, or ignorance of the law, he ruins the litigant coming before him-would not the litigant in that case be as much entitled, as a result of your error of judgment in appointing that judge, to receive compensation from the Government as the depositors of the Farmers Bank are to-day? The unfortunate appointment was made by the Government of a man supposed to be well versed in the law and to be honest, and yet the momen' he sits on the Bench he becomes dishonest, displays ignorance of the law, and as a consequence he ruins the litigants by his judgments-I ask again have not the litigants recourse against the Government? If we must accept the dictum of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in the case of the Farmers Bank depositors the ruined litigants would have logically the same recourse. I think that this legislation, as my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) stated a moment ago, creates a grave precedent, and if my hon. friend refers to the conservative press of the country-1and when I use the word ' conservative ' I apply it not only to the press of the Conservative persuasion, but, in its proper and wider sense-he will find that this legislation is very much deplored indeed. In my judgment, if the Government must reimburse the Farmers Bank depositors, the depositors of the Banque du Peuple, the Banque Ville Marie and La Banque St. Jean-my electors-should receive similar treatment, and for my part, I will try and see that they agitate to get justice the same as the Farmers Bank depositors have.

Will my hon. friend allow me; the Ville-Marie bank, let it be well understood, because we have enough sins of our own to answer for, was not a French-Canadian bank. It had a French-Canadian name only.

Then let me put it generally, and speaking generally I say that I do not believe there should be one law for one part of the country and another law for another part of the country, in matters of this sort!
Although the Ville-Marie bank was not a French-Canadian bank, the French-Canadian people lost heavily.

One of my friends beside me says that there is not one law for one part of the country and another law for another part of the country. My opinion is that this is making one law in one case and none in another. That may be a question of judgment, and I am only giving my judgment this afternoon. Through a very peculiar coincidence I happen to hold two shares in the Farmers Bank, which, of course, was a mere trifle, but the most careful inquiry I had been able to make when that bank went into liquidation convinced me that the loss was all due to Travers' irregularities and not to any irregularity on the part of the Government; and, that while the ex-Minister of Finance was probably somewhat careless in the granting of the certificate, yet, after that certificate was
issued, if the management of the bank had been honest and proper, there would not have been any loss, but the bank would have been a success. In my judgment, the efficient and proximate cause of the failure was not the granting of the certificate but the irregularity and criminal conduct of the management.

Some of these gentlemen, Mr. Chairman, are going too far afield. If you look at what occurred immediately after the certificate was given, you will find out who was liable and who was not. Where the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Niekle) is at fault is that he does not distinguish between (negligence and gross negligence. It is quite true that ordinary common negligence may not'imply responsibility, but gross negligenoe is an entirely different thing, and I contend that in this case there certainly was very gross negligence.
How do you know?

I am stating my case, and if the hon. gentleman will wait I will tell him more. Therefore, we have to deal with the question of gross negligence. Now, then, is the extraordinary principle to be laid down that a Government is above all liability, that it may blunder, that it may do the most stupid things, that it may in fact do criminal things, and yet not be responsible?
Mr-. NICKLE:	Is it not correct in law
to say that a petition of right could issue to permit the trial of the responsibility of a government for the negligence of an official?

I think it is, but that is entirely contrary to what the hon. gentleman has just said. According to my understanding there can be no question in the mind of the ordinary citizen that the Government that undertakes to do a thing, by the very fact that it has undertaken to do it-incurs a co-relative responsibility, if it undertakes to issue a certificate. If it states that a bank can go on without a certificate, well and good, but where the Government says that a bank cannot go on without a certificate and prescribes the rules for the issuance of that certificate, there is beyond all question a responsibility upon the Government to see that no gross negligence is committed. To say that the efficient cause is subsequent to the issuance of a

certificate, is to say that had a thief who stole the money and run been caught as he might have been caught as he ran through the streets, the loss would not have occurred. But that is an entirely different proposition.
When did the hon. gentleman contend that this gross negligence took place? Was it ^during the administration of the bank, after it commenced business, or before?

It certainly was before the certificate had issued. As I understand the evidence, it was pointed out very clearly that a full and complete warning was given to the people who had the power to issue the certificate, but notwithstanding that fact, when they should have been alert to catch every sound of warning, especially in such an affair as this, they absolutely glossed it all over and issued a certificate, and it was because they issued that certificate an!d because of the right of the bank to transact business that the people of this country put their money in the bank on the assurance that the Government was transacting its business properly, and so lost their money. It had nothing whatever to do with Travers; it had nothing whatever to do with the management of the bank; the fact is that because the certificate had been granted the people put their money in the bank.
What about the shareholders?

They of course are supposed to look into the management of the bank themselves. They are one with Travers, in my opinion, and whilst they cannot be charged with criminal negligence, they certainly ought to be charged with gross negligence, and ought not to get anything at all. They have been mulcted to the extent of their double liability, and quite properly so. That is my opinion upon that. As to French-Canadian banks, are we to be threatened? I say that whether they are French-Canadian banks or not, if the money is stolen from the people under the circumstances of this case, they should get their money.
Why not?

Certainly, why not. But the idea set out by prominent gentlemen sitting in this House, that if other institutions are not recouped, nothing shall be done for the people who suffered in this case, is the most monstrous doctrine I have

ever heard. And the converse is true: if right is done in this case, it must be done in every case; if these other banks, on investigation, are proven to be in the same position as this bank, then pay the people their money. But do not let it go abroad that the poor people of this country, relying on the certificate of a Government, may put their money on deposit in a bank -and are to have no reliance on, the Government and no recourse when their money is taken from them. Are we to understand that a Government may be grossly negligent, yes, even inhumanly negligent, and sti'll escape liability? And yet that is the doctrine that is laid -down here to-day by some hon. gentlemen.

If the debate is to go on at this -stage, I do not see why I should not make a few observations. I quite approve of the -stand taken by my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mr. Ross), but I quite disapprove of hi-s reason for taking that -stand. I do not think there could be any excuse for this Government, or for any government, coming to the aid of any bank for the reason that that bank had been improperly managed, or that there has been subsequent loss through the mismanagement, or incompetency, or fraud, or anything else of that sort. I would not support this Government if they tried to recompense the depositors for that reason. I support the Government for the reason given by the Minister of Finance, namely, that the certificate was wrongfully obtained, and that the initial mistake was made by the late Government in granting the certificate. Any person who has read the evidence can come to no other conclusion than that there was absolute lack of care and caution on the part of the Treasury Board. That can be stated without singling out any individual, and particularly the late Minister of Finance. To say that there was no negligence is to overlook the fact that the ex-Minister of Finance him-self was warned as to the process by which the subscriptions were being received by Mr. Traver-s and others. And, as to there being political reasons for thi-s action, there are no political reasons that do not apply to both parties. Hon. gentlemen who heard read the list of names of the depositors in that bank, will remember that the very first reference was to the township of Zorra, represented by my hon. friend from North -Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). A large number were in the eon-

*stituency represented by my hen, friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross).

Does the hon. member
mean to say that the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) made the promise?
No. Nor did I.
There was not a large number mentioned from my riding; there was not one single name.

As far as differentiating
between the shareholders and the depositors is concerned, I do not think for one minute that the shareholders should be considered at all. A shareholder is a man who enters into a business of that sort as an investor. He knows what he is doing; he becomes a proprietor of the bank; he knows that there is a double liability. He knows the hazard of his venture, because he makes an investment on which there is a double liability; but the depositor, in almost every case when he deposits his money in a chartered bank, believes he is depositing it there for safekeeping, and that the stability of this country is behind the bank. At any rate, he used to believe that, before the failure of the Farmers Bank. I cannot see where my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) finds any logic whatever in making a parallel between this and a judgment given by a judge which may ruin a litigant, although the judge may have been improperly appointed by this Government. In that case a litigant has more than one appeal against the judgment of that particular judge. In any event it is not a parallel case. I do not approve of my hon. friend the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) stating that this is a pernicious and obnoxious precedent. It is not a precedent for such cases as advanced by my hon. friend the member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). No person has ever alleged that any of these banks obtained their certificates through fraudulent means. No person has ever contended that the certificates granted to these banks weTe obtained from the Minister of Finance or the Treasury Board after the Treasury Board had been warned that wrongful practices were being resorted to for the purpose of procuring deposits. It will be a precedent, and I hope that it will be observed as a precedent, if the Minister of Finance of the present day or of any future time shall issue a certificate to a number of men who are organizing a bank and who have
obtained a charter or a certificate to do business for that bank in the same way that Mr. Travers and others did in connection with the Farmers Bank.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. W. T. White thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 185, for the relief of the depositors of the Farmers Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) moved second reading of Bill No. 183, to provide for the payment of a yearly allowance to Mrs. Alice Joynson, widow of the late J. H. Joynson, a guard in the British Columbia penitentiary.
Perhaps the minister will make a very short statement of the occasion, and there may be no discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The matter was discussed somewhat fully when the resolution on which the Bill is based was before the House. The purpose is to provide an annuity for the lady mentioned who is the widow of a man who was a gum d in the British Columbia penitentiary. Something over a year ago, this man was killed in endeavouring to prevent the escape from the penitentiary of two very desperate criminals. In their endeavour to escape, one of the criminals was killed and, very unfortunately, this man Joynson was also killed. I may say that his conduct on the occasion showed what I think may be properly described as conspicuous bravery. These two desperate men had succeeded, in the first place, in depriving one of the guards of the penitentiary, who was in immediate supervision over them, of his revolver, and then, by threatening other guards as they passed through different portions of the penitentiary grounds with this revolver, they succeeded in possessing themselves of the revolvers of those guards too. They had reached the final gates which separated them from liberty and were threatening the guards upon the wall when this man Joynson came to the rescue and at the risk, and, as it proved, at the price of his own life, intervened to prevent the escape. He has left a widow who has some small children and who is not in a position to maintain herself. Therefore we propose to give her a small annuity of $500 a year, the money to be paid to her monthly.

In connection with
this Bill, as I unintentionally did an injustice to my hon. friend the Postmaster General the other day in referring to the Oka Case, I wish to state most emphatically that I read this morning the fourth volume of the debates of 1911-12, after the explanation made by my hon. friend, and he is right in his explanation. When we discussed that case in the House, the hon. member for Two Mountains (Mr. Ethier) asked that certain provision be made for the widow and that the mail contract be given to her. I see by ' Hansard ' that my hon. friend said at the time that it was not possible to give the contract, because the children were too young and the people objected to that contract being handed to minors. He said, however, at that time that he would see at the next session or at the earliest opportunity-it was in the dying days of the session-that a certain amount would be paid to the widow as a gratuity, and this morning I saw the cheque. I beg to apologize to the hon. minister for making the statement I did.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the chair. [DOT]
On section 1-pension for Mrs. Joynson:
On what principle did the hon. gentleman fix the compensation in this case? Is this a certain proportion of the salary of the deceased?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The man was earning at the time $700 a year. We allowed Mrs. Joynson last year the salary for that year. Now, we are allowing $500. Perhaps it is a little difficult to say that there is any principle upon which we fixed it, save that it may be said that this family were living on $700, and there was the man himself to maintain. We know that less than $500 would not be worth while, and that this sum will at least help this woman and her children.

I endorse what the minister has done in this matter; and should such an unfortunate case arise in the future, I hope there would be no hesitation in making proportionately liberal provision for the surviving dependents, and I would much rather the error should be on the side of liberality than on the side of economy.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.	,

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee on Bill No. 114, to amend the Indian Act.-Mr. Roche. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-power to establish industrial schools, etc. :

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When this Bill was before the House on the last occasion when I was present, it was pointed out that this section might be interpreted to be rather wider than it was intended by the department to be. It was stated that any school to which was committed an Indian child might be considered an industrial school within the meaning of this section. That was not the design. In accordance with the suggestion made on that occasion by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), I beg to move the following in lieu of that section:
The Governor in Council may establish an industrial school or a boarding school for Indians, or may declare any school or Institution where children are provided with board and lodging as well as instruction and with the managing authorities of which the superintendent general has made an agreement for the admission of an Indian child or children and for the inspection of the school or Institution, to be an industrial school or boarding school for the purpose of this or the next following section.
This provides that where an arrangement has been made between the superintendent general and the authorities of the school, that is, where it is mutually agreeable, it can be done.
That meets the objection, so far as I am concerned.

I would like to have it clearer that this agreement spoken of is not merely an agreement as to the maintenance and control of that child, but is an agreement as to the measure of control of the school by the Government in consideration of the aid given.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, that is the idea.
That is the purport of the agreement ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 2-taking land for schools:

When this section was up the other night, I criticised it on the ground that it seemed to me that the occasion was trifling as a warrant for interference with the rights of the Indian to his land. I think that possibly some isolated instance has

occurred, and it is proposed to cure the difficulty by legislation. But I think it would be better to allow the individual difficulty to remain rather than to interfere by legislation with the ownership of land by the Indian. There is nothing upon which the Indians are quite so touchy as the ownership of land, and it is not well to interfere with them in any way unless the circumstances make it unavoidable.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This is because of a certain difficulty having arisen where land was nee'ded and was refused by the Indian. Of course, it is not intended that the land should be taken without compensation. We are not very particular about securing this power, but we think that in case of similar difficulty arising it is better that this should be passed rather than see a school blocked.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-withdrawal of half-breed from treaty; status of wife:

When this section was under consideration the other night, I mentioned the fact that under recent conditions-I am not sure whether under present conditions or not-half-breed scrip is issued to members of bands who withdraw from those bands. If there is no issue of scrip, if that absolutely does not exist, the objection I make does not hold. But if half-breed scrip is issued to members of bands who withdraw from those bands, then the effect of this section would be to double the object of the scrip speculator in securing the withdrawal of the members from the band by automatically withdrawing the wife with the husband. Either the woman would be entitled to the scrip or she would lose the benefit of being in the band. Either one or other would be detrimental to the interest of the half-breeds.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have read the hon. member's criticism on this point. It is not the intention to issue any further scrip. The issue of scrip has ceased, and will not be made in the future.
How long is it since any scrip has been issued?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: None has been issued within the last two or three years.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6-compulsory, etc., sale of reserve:
Has the hon. minister considered the protest of the Caughnawaga Indians on this subject?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think the Caughnawaga Indians are unnecessarily alarmed.
What is the effect of the clause?	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have already an amendment, by which there is a portion of a reserve that is required for some public purpose, adjacent to a city or town of 8,000 population, and where the Indians refuse to surrender and are absolutely preventing the development of that portion of the country, provision was taken by my predecessor to have a reference to a judge of the Exchequer Court for inquiry and report to the Governor in Council, which report is placed before Parliament and must be passed upon	by	Parliament beforethe Governor	in	Council can act.
The Act is being further amended by doing away with the limitation to cities and towns of a population of 8,000 or more, so that wherever lands are required for similar purposes, they shall, where the indians refuse to surrender, be dealt with in a similar way. There is no design upon the Caughnawaga reserve; the amendment introduced in 1911 has never been called into requisition and this one may never be called into requisition. There is no danger of the Caugbna-wagans losing their reserve.

I am glad to accept the word of my hon, friend in that regard. The Chief of the Caughnawaga band wrote the letter which I read the other day in the House, but after my hon. friend's assurance that they need not be nervous about any sinister design on his part, I suppose they will now be satisfied.
What is the procedure in the obtaining of portions of Indian reserves not in or near a town, for industrial purposes? Is it complicated?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In such cases we secure a surrender from the Indians.
What is the procedure?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We send one of our officials to the reserve, and he calls a meeting of the band and places the proposition before them. A vote is secured, and all that is necessary is the assent of the majority of the band. No protracted time is required and there is no complication.
Is conveyance made by the chief of the Indian tribe?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

The rumour is prevalent that an effort is to be made to take the Restigouehe reserve, or a large portion of it, for the establishment of a mill. The reserve is opposite the town of Campbellton, in the province of New Brunswick. In this case, it is not the town but some industrial corporation that is asking for further taking over of the reserve.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I understand that in the
past there have been some negotiations between the owners or proprietors of the proposed mill and the Indians, but the Indians have thus far refused to surrender.
It would seem that under this section the company can get the reserve by going to the Exchequer Cojirt.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Not unless the proposed
establishment is considered by the Exchequer Court to be a public utility.

The Baie des Chaleurs
Milling Company are located on the reserve at the present time. There is a rumour that these people are looking for a site for a pulp mill along the Restigouehe river and that they have taken up several options. It is openly stated that they are going to locate on this reserve and I would like to know from the minister Whether any application has been received in this regard.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is true that so far as the mill is concerned they have an old lease from the Indian Department, but it would be impossible for that company to step in and take away any portion of the reserve without the consent of the Indians, from whom they must secure formal surrender. This provision distinctly states that the matter shall be referred to the Exchequer Court of Canada for inquiry and report as to whether the taking over of any portion of the reserve is expedient and as to whether the interests of the public and of the Indians of the'band will thereby be served.

Formerly, if the Indians
refused to surrender, that was the end of it, but now any company desiring to obtain the land may go to the Exchequer Court and, by following the necessary process, oan get the reserve or any portion of it. Campbelton is not a town having a population of 8,000 and it seems to me that under this legislation the company will be able to get this reserve.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is, I
think, confounding private enterprises with public utility. .

It may be declared that
this private enterprise is a public utility. Although the minister may not know it, I am satisfied that some person may take advantage of this provision. ,

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that if this case were brought before the Exchequer Court the supreme authority is, after all, the Parliament of Canada. Parliament must pass upon it favourably before any action can be taken.

Whether or not it is intended to furnish means by
5 p.m. which, this oan be done, it is the intention of that industry that it is to be done. These Indians would thereby be dispossessed; they would be forced out of their lands, which would be turned over to this company by the usual process.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have not in mind the
case to which my hon. friend refers.
Mil-. CARVELL:	The minister will remember that early in the session I asked him some questions with regard to the Tobi-qne reserve. As my hon. friend knows, the valuable timber upon one portion of that reserve was pretty well cleaned off by his friend, Mr. Smith, during the last year, but the upper portion of the reserve still has a considerable amount of valuable timber.
I am afraid that under thi3 section the remainder of the lumber may be appropriated by gentlemen who require it in their business. One gentleman said that he had a mill a few miles down the river and as the lumber would be worth a little more to him than to anybody else, he ought to have it. I would like to know if the minister thinks this section is strong enough to allow.these gentlemen; to come in and gather up the remainder of the Tobique Indian reserve.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think not. It is not designed to cover a case of that kind and I am satisfied in my own mind that it would not cover it.

I lam glad indeed to
hear that, and I hope the minister will give us a promise that the remainder of the Tobique Indian' reserve will not be gathered in by the politicians of New Brunswick,

the same ,as the southern portion of the reserve has already been gathered in.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think probably the hon. gentleman has in view the gathering in, as he calls it, of certain timber that is upon the reserve. Certain lands were disposed of from time to time before this Government came into power, and recently a portion of the timber was sold, but that has nothing whatever to do with this provision of the Act. Every case will be dealt with on its merits. It is not my present intention to alienate any other portion of the Tobique reserve, and I am sure that unless they can make ont a very good case it wall not be done.

I am glad to hear that.
I do not want to discuss just now the details of what is taking place because I think this is not the proper occasion, and I hope to have an occasion of doing so before prorogation. The minister will understand, however, that we have alienated portions of this reserve and, according to the returns, alienated it without much rhyme or reason, and so far as I can see without any application on the part of the persons who purchased it. The matter seemed to be the suggestion of the minister's own department that this land should be sold to Mr. Smith. I only hope that no more suggestions like that will be made, and that what remains of the Indian reserve will be maintained for the Indians and not for the benefit of the politicians.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It was surrendered by the Indians.

I understand that a
portion of the land on the south of the Tobique river had been surrendered by some arrangement so that the department was in a position to sell; but the department was not in a position to give this land over to a political supporter without public competition and without the public knowing anything about it; and giving it to him for one-quarter of what the land was worth and allowing him to steal what valuable timber there was on it. Surely the department was not justified in doing that. However, I shall discuss that later.

Has it come to the knowledge of the minister that there is an Indian reserve in the city of Sydney upon which certain individuals have been casting envious eyes for some years? I understand that applications, in one form or another, 223i
have been made-or were made, at all events, to the late Minister of the Interior- and I think the efforts in that direction have been continued up to a comparatively recent date.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Propositions have been
made to the department on more than one occasion to have the Indians moved from their present location in the town of Sydney to some other place. The Indians have not been agreeable to such a transfer and, therefore, the department have not proceeded with the case at all. The Indians are not being disturbed, and will not be disturbed without their consent.
Will the passage of this Act make it easier to remove the Indians from that reserve ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not unless it is desired to use the land for some public purpose. The judge of the Exchequer Court must first decide that it is a question not only of expediency but in the interests of the public as well as in the interests of the Indians. This amendment is not designed to cover that particular case, or any case like it. Propositions have come in to the department about that reserve, but invariably the Indians have refused to surrender their land, and that settles it so far as the department is concerned. We have no intention of calling this Act into requisition in order to dispossess them of their land.
I understand the minister to say that it is only in the event of the land being required for public purposes that the Indians may be ultimately removed.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I might say to my hon. friend that the amendment brought in in 1911 would cover this particular case, because Sydney has a population of 8,000 people.
So if this Act is passed, it will not be any easier to get rid of the Indians than heretofore ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not at all.

The minister so intends to administer the Act that the land will not be sold unless it is required in the public interests. I am afraid, however, that the Bill does not very happily cover the minister's intentions, and it is possible that at some future date there will be another minister of the Interior not possessed of the same high ideals as the present one. If the minister will read section 6 carefully he will see that it is not

confined to the case of a public body requiring the land. It 'says:
In a case of an Indian reserve which adjoins or is situated wholly or partly within an incorporated town or city or in the immediate neighbourhood thereof or which contains more land than is necessary for the use of the band-
That is the point.
-or which is so situated as to materially retard the natural development of the surrounding country-[DOT]
But, to go bacik a moment, it says: 'which contains more land than is necessary for the use of the band.' It seems to me that the minister should eliminate that line from the Bill, because you can hardly find an Indian reserve in the Dominion in regard to which some enterprising gentleman will not be convinced that they have more land than is required for the use of the band, and, once he convinces the minister that such is the case, he then has a right to apply for it. The .section goes on:
-which reserve has not been released or surrendered by the Indians and which the Indians refuse to surrender, the Governor in Council may, upon the recommendation of the Superintendent General, refer to the Exchequer Court of Canada for inquiry and report the question as to whether it is expedient, having regard to the interest of the public and of the Indians of the,band for whose use the reserve is held, that the whole or any portion of the said reserve should be sold for the benefit of the Indians, and that the Indians should be removed from the reserve or any part of it.
To go back to the Tobique Indian reserve, to which I have already referred. There are thousands of acres in that reserve that the Indians do not occupy. They occupy only a very small portion of me reserve; I think I am safe in saying that nine-tenths of the reserve is entirely in forest land, and I can quite understand how a number of enterprising gentlemen from New Brunswick may come here and convince-not this minister, because he has had a little experience of them-the minister's successor-that there is more land there than is necessary for the use of the Indians, and therefore persuade him to sell, not the whole of it, but the portion that has valuable timber. Those words in lines 21 and 22 of .section 6 on page 2 are the ones to which I object. I am afraid it is opening up a very wide field indeed.
I can readily understand that, in the case of an Indian reserve situated right in the midst of a town, there may be very strong reasons why that reserve .should be opened to the public and the Indians removed to IMr. Carvell].
some other place. There would be strong reasons for that if some public utility required it, for instance, but I think this section leaves it open for any private individual who casts covetous eyes upon a portion of an Indian reserve to come to the minister, and possibly work the oracle and get possession of the property.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman overlooks this fact. The Minister of the Interior, no matter who he may be, has not power to sell the Indian reserve. The matter would have to be referred to the judge of the Exchequer Court who makes a full inquiry. Witnesses are examined under oath and the Indians are represented by counsel paid for by the department. The judge, after inquiring fully into the matter, makes his report to Parliament; and if Parliament pass upon it, the case goes to the Governor in Council for final action. That is exactly the procedure that took place under the late Administration. Parliament must pass upon it before it goes to the Governor in Council.
We know what Parliament means; we had an illustration of that, this afternoon, in connection with the Farmers Bank.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will
have a chance to enter his protest if it is proposed to sell any part of a reserve.
And that is all.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We often have the jurisdiction of the Governor in Council called in question, and hear it said that this and that matter ought to be brought to the high court of Parliament. As I said, the Minister of the Interior, no matter who he may be, has no jurisdiction in the matter of selling an Indian reserve. All he can do is to refeT it to the Exchequer Court. It is then reported upon to Parliament, and Parliament passes upon it before the Governor in Council takes final action; so that I do not s>ee any force in the hon. gentleman's objection. No undue influence can be brought to bear upon the Minister of the Interior, for he simply cannot act.	1

Parliament is to-day laying down the law which will control the judge of the Exchequer Court when the question is brought before him. Parliament is contemplating to-day that, if there is more land in the Indian reserves than the Indians are using, the extra area may be taken from them on an order of the judge. It is perfectly clear that if a case in regard to a certain Indian reserve is

brought before the Exchequer Court, and if it is proven that there is more land in the Indian reserve than the Indians are beneficially using, the judge will have no discretion but to declare that a portion of the reserve shall toe taken from the Indians. That is the whole purpose of the Bill, that is what it says, that is what will be the necessary result. I maintain that this is most objectionable.
Will that apply to any reserve?

Yes. I think that the minister will realize that in pressing this legislation on Parliament he is proposing to destroy the treaty rights of the Indians by authority of Parliament. I am quite aware that Parliament can destroy these treaty rights but I am not prepared to admit that Parliament ought to. The minister may say that under the late Government provision was made for the taking of the land from the Indians toy the order of the Exchequer Court. It is quite true. A Bill was brought before Parliament by myself, as an emergency measure, after a complete declaration of the fact that it was trespassing upon the treaty rights of the Indians, and that it was a question as to which was the greater right and which was the greater wrong. It was particularly provided in the Bill that it should only have effect where, by reason of the proximity of a large population, the land occupied by the Indians had reached an abnormal cash value and the Indians in occupation were not receiving adequate benefit, and where the duty of the Government, as guardians of the Indians, required them to take such action as would ensure to them all of the increased value by reason of the proximity to a large population. That was the limitation under which that extraordinary power could be exercised through the courts. But my hon. friend departs from that extraordinary condition altogether and in any circumstances where any Indian reserve occupies a greater area than the Indians are using he can put this Act into operation and the judge of the Exchequer Court must act as he is directed by the terms of this section. In so far as the Minister desires to excuse this Bill by suggesting that its terms are parallel with the terms of the Act now on the statute book, I desire to repudiate the parallel absolutely and to say that the Act now on the statute book is within limitations which absolutely safeguard the rights of the Indians and that it was put there for the direct benefit of the Indians. This
Bill is certainly a trespass upon the rights of the Indians wherever they may be located throughout Canada.
There is another feature of this Indian question that I am going to take an opportunity of directing to the attention of the minister. This Bill is a trespass upon the ordinary treaty rights of the Indians. But there are the bands of the Six Nation Indians located on the Grand river in Ontario who, I maintain, are in a different legal position from any Indian bands who are native to the country. These Indian bands on the Grand river had their original home in the United States. At the close of die war of the revolution they emigrated to Canada and were given lands under a special treaty, not as subjects of Great Britain, but as allies of Great Britain, and I maintain that the holding of these Six Nation Indians on the Grand river is of such a kind that this Parliament has no right to interfere with it. I admit that Parliament has the power to interfere with the rights of Indians under treaty made with this Government, but I say that this Parliament has no right to interfere with a treaty made between the Imperial Government and the Six Nation Indians.
I protest most strongly against this legislation as being a breaking of faith with the Indians in a matter in which faith should be most sacredly kept. The other night, speaking in the House, I referred to the nature of the Indian and to the necessity of maintaining his self-respect. The knowledge of the ownership of his land is the greatest factor in maintaining his self-respect, and if we are to let him understand that the land which he is located upon and which is sacred to himself and his tribe is not his excepting as the Parliament or Government of the day may see fit to declare, you simply take away the last vestige of his self-respect, the last opportunity to save in him all that makes him a man.

I wish to emphasize the attitude taken by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) as regards the sacredness of the title which the Indians have to their reserves. I was speaking a moment ago of the Caughna-waga Indians, and my hon. friend said that there was no sinister motive behind this clause 6 as regards their reserve. Looking over the documents which were published by this Government many years ago, I find the titles to the reserves, and I submit that even with

the legislation which is before the House to-day, the department could not dispossess the Caughnawaga band of that reserve or any part of it. I would refer my hon. friend the minister to the titles to the Sault Sit. Louis reserve in the ' Indian Treaties and Surrenders/ vols 1 and 2, officially published in the year 1891, and which contains the Indian treaties and surrenders from 1680 to 1890.
Respecting the Caughnawaga reserve, the following document is, I believe the most ancient concession made by France to the Indians of Canada. It will be seen from it that the Caughnawaga reserve was originally granted to the Jesuit Fathers by Louis aIV, on the 29th of May, 1680. Here are the terms of the grant:
Fontainebleau, France, 29th May, 1680.
Louis, by the Grace of God, King of France and of Navarre. To all to whom these presents may come, greeting:
Our dearest and well beloved, the Religious Order of the Society of Jesus, residing in our Dominion of New France, have caused it to be most humbly represented to us that the lands of the Prairie de la Magdalene, which were heretofore granted to them, being too damp for the purpose of sowing and of providing for the sustenance of the Iroquois who have thereon settled, and that it is feared they might leave if we were not pleased to give them the land called 'Le Sault' containing two leagues in width from a point opposite the St. Louis rapids, going up along the lake by an equal depth, with two islands, islets and shoals, which are in front and adjoining the lands of the said Prairie de la Magdalene, which would allow them not only to receive the said Iroquois but even to increase their number, and to spread by that means the knowledge of faith and of the Gospel; for these reasons, desiring to contribute to the conversion and instruction of the said Iroquois and to deal favourably with the said petitioners, we have made and do make them a donation by these presents signed with our hand, of the said land called *Le Sault' containing two leagues, in width from a point opposite the St. Louis rapids, going up along the lake, by an equal depth, with two islands, islets and shoals, which are in front and adjoining the lands of the Prairie de la Magdalene on condition that the said land called 'Le Sault' shall belong to us, when the said Iroquois will, give it up, toute d6frich6e (free and clear as it then may be without any claims on us).
We permit and allow all those who wish to bring to the said Iroquois rings, knives and other small mercery and such things, to do so; we do most expressly prohibit and forbid the French who may live with or go among the said Iroquois and other Indian nations who may settle on the said land called 'Le Sault' from having and keeping any cattle, and all persons from keeping any public-house among the dwellings (dans le bourg) of the said Iroquois which may be built on the said land.
Therefore we order our beloved and faithful men holding our Sovereign Court at Quebec, and all our other judicial officers whom it may
fMr. Lemieux.]
concern, to have these presents our letters of donation and of grant read and registered and to permit the said petitioners to use and enjoy the same, ceasing and putting a stop to all troubles and hindrances which might be caused to them to the contrary, for such is our pleasure.
In faith whereof we have signed these presents and affixed our Seals.
Given at Fontainebleau the twrenty-ninth day of May in the year of Grace one thousand six hundred and eighty and of our reign the thirty-eighth.
(Signed) Louis.
By the King.
(Signed) Colbert.
Later on Frontenac, one of the most illustrious governors under the French regime, issued the following letters patent, dated Quebec, 31st of October, 1680:
Quebec, 31st October, 1680.
With regard to what was represented to us by the Reverend Fathers of the Society of Jesus, that His Majesty by his letters patent of the twenty-ninth of May one thousand six hundred and eighty, registered at the Sovereign Council at Quebec on the twenty-ninth of October ensuing, having made to them a gift of the land called 'Le Sault' containing two leagues in width from a point opposite the St. Louis rapids going up along the lake, by an equal depth, with two islands, islets and shoals which are in front, and adjoining the lands of the Prairie de la Magdalene, for the reasons mentioned in said letters and in the clauses and conditions therein laid; and whereas they have asked that we might be pleased to grant them a piece of land of one league	and a half	or	thereabouts	in lengthto be	taken from	the	said land	called 'LeSault' going up along the lake, towards the seigniority of Chateauguay, by two leagues in depth, which would afford them a still better	opportunity	of	drawing thereto the
Iroquois and other Indians, to increase their number and to spread by that means the knowledge of faith and of the Gospel;
We, by virtue of the power given to us conjointly by His Majesty, and in order to facilitate still more the said Reverend Fathers of the	Society of	Jesus with the	means of
continuing the care and pains which they have been doing for a long time and with such zeal, for the conversion and instruction of the said Iroquois and other Indians, we have given, granted and conceded, do give, grant and concede to them by these presents, the said piece of land of about one league and a half in length, to be taken from the said land called 'Le Sault' extending toward the seigniority of Chateauguay, by two leagues in depth, to be used and enjoyed by the said Reverend Fathers on the same conditions, clauses and terms as are set forth in the aforesaid letters patent of His Majesty, and that they shall obtain from him a ratification of the presents in a year from to-day.
In faith whereof we have signed these presents and affixed the seal of our arms.
Given at Quebec, on the thirty-first of October, one thousand six hundred and eighty.
(Signed) Frontenac.
(Signed) Duchesneau.

This is signed by Frontenac, and Duches-neau who was Intendant of New France.
Looking over these historic documents, I find that later on the Iroquois had a litigation with the Jesuit Fathers, just at the beginning of British domination. The case was brought up before the administrators of the colony at that time. After the conquest the country was divided into three governments : the Government of Montreal, the Government of Three Bivers, and the Government of Quebec, and the question came up in 1762 before His Excellency Thomas Gage, Governor of Montreal, assisted by his Council.
22nd March, 1762.
Before His Excellency Thomas Gage, Governor of Montreal, assisted by His Council, to wit, Messrs. Frederick Haldimand, Colonel of the 4th Battalion of the Royal American, and William Browning, Major of the 46th Regiment, Herbert Munster, Major of the 4th Battalion of the Royal American, and Gabriel Christie, Major and Quarter-Master of His Majesty's Armies.
Between the Iroquois Indians and other Indians of Sault St. Louis, appearing by Mr. Clauss their Attorney, Plaintiff, on the one
part:
And the Very Reverend Fathers of the Society of Jesus, appearing by the Reverend Father Wett, their Attorney, Defendant, on the other part.
One of the chief allegations of the Iroquois in that famous litigation was:
That at the surrender of this country all things had been well arranged to maintain the said Indians in possession of their lands at Sault St. Louis, but that now the Jesuit Fathers, their missionaries, were granting continually to the French the lands forming part of the territory of Sault St. Louis which, however, they believed belonged to them by a title of grant given them by His Most Christian Majesty. And that if matters are not promptly set right, they would soon see themselves obliged to give up their own fields, to withdraw with their families to the woods, considering they do not any longer find there enough land to afford a means of living.
The Indians were also claiming some of the church property. They claimed that they had paid their share to the maintenance of the church, and that they were entitled to its ornaments and perquisites. Judgment was rendered by that special tribunal presided over by His Excellency Thomas Gage, and perhaps it would be well to read what the decision was:
We are of opinion that the grant of the lands of Sault St. Louis was made to the Right Reverend Jesuit Fathers with the sole intention of settling these Iroquois and other Indians and that all the soil could produce was wholly intended for their profit and advantage. The reasons which the Right Reverand Jesuit Fathers use in their petition, and which seemed to have determined His Most Christian Majesty
to make his grant, were founded on the fear that the Iroquois that had settled at that time on the Seigniory of Laprairie and occupied lands which were too damp for the purpose of sowing, should happen to leave, alleging that by means of that new grant, they would be not only kept back but that their number would be increased and by that means the knowledge of faith and of the Gospel would be spread.
And another paragraph as follows:
Therefore we deprive and nonsuit the Right Reverend Jesuit Fathers of all temporal rights which they might have assumed on the said lands either by the condescension of the Governors or the Tntendants, the only title by which they have got the decrees of Union to the estate which they obtained at different times, or by right of possession or other reasons which they might allege, and we order that the said Indians of the Sault-
Our English-speaking friends would do well to keep the pronunciation of the word ' Sault' not ' Soa'
-be put in possession of and do enjoy peaceably for themselves their heirs and other Indians who would like to join them, the whole land and revenue which the said concession can produce.
And being of opinion that nothing contributes more efficaciously to civilize and enlighten the Indian nation than by scrupulously keeping the pledges which are made with them, and by preventing all cause of disagreement between them, and the inhabitants settled in their neighbourhood.
We order that the boundaries of the concession of the Iroquois of the Sault be drawn as soon as possible by a sworn surveyor, and that the limit of said concession be marked with stones fastened into the earth and stamped with His Britannic Majesty's Arms, and that the figurative plan thereof be delivered at a record office.
And then the litigation is settled by the representatives of His Majesty, the new King of British North America, deeding this reserve to the Iroquois, their heirs' and successors, because it had been deeded to them for their purposes by the Crown of France in 1680. This constitutes an Imperial title. The Caughnawaga Indians received first a royal title from the Crown of France, and after the conquest, it was implemented by another royal title. By the treaties and by the capitulations of Montreal and Quebec, reference is made to the title of the Indians in their reserves as established by the Crown of France. Therefore in a case of this kind such as Caughnawaga reserve, I do not believe that this Parliament or the Department of Indian Affairs could interfere in any way, manner or form. My hon. friend has declared that the Iroquois should have no fear, but it is well that the country should know that this reserve was given under Louis XIV and confirmed by George III after the conquest, and that the Government takes authority to-alter the conditions

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is perfectly obvious
that great c-are must be taken in dealing with the titles of the Indians, and it is the desire of the Government to carry out that principle. As far -as the legal point Which my hon. friend has made is concerned, I am not at the moment quite lalble to- appreciate it, because the result of it would be that any title acquired in this country to land, which is based upon the Acts of the British Crown or of the French Crown -before responsible government was introduced into this -country, could not be the subject of expropriation at all, whether it -belonged to the Indians or to any one else. I do net conceive that to -be the law of this country, nor do I think that the powers of Parliament are limited in that way. Under the British system, the title of all lands is traced to the Crown; -and it does not make any difference, so far as the legal aspect is concerned, Whether the title is traced, to the Crown before we have responsible government in this country or whether it is traced to the Crown afterwards, through the medium of responsible government. The position is precisely the same. Parliament has the right to declare in respect of the ordinary citizen of the country that his 'lands may be taken, with suitable compensation, for purposes of -a public character. It goes further than that:	It empowers corporations
carrying on public utilities to expropriate lands of ordinary citizens, without their consent but with due compensation, for such public purposes. As far as the Indians

are concerned, the object of this legislation is simply to extend in a certain measure a principle which has -already been acted upon by this Parliament in a measure introduced, I think, by my hon. friend the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) a few years ago. It is simply extending the conditions under which that power may be exercised in the public interest.
It is extending it much beyond the purview of public interest and public utility; it is getting down to where private individuals -are interested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not understand the legislation just in the way that the hon. member for Garleton understands it. Section 49a, which is the amending section, begins in this way:
In the case of an Indian reserve which adjoins or is situated wholly or partly within an incorporated town or city or in the immediate neighbourhood thereof or which contains more land than is necessary for the use of the band or which is so situated as to materially retard the natural development of the surrounding country.
Then certain procedure cam be followed for the purpose of expropriating the land without a surrender by the Indians. It is all concerned with questions of the public interest, land the Minister of the Crown who undertakes the initiating of proceedings must, of course, have due regard to what those are. In any case, the land of the Indians can only be taken after proper proceedings have been had in the Exchequer Court of Canada and under conditions which safeguard the interests of the Indians in every respect. They must be paid for their improvements; they must be fully compensated in every way; and further than that, if I remember the section correctly, they must be provided with certain suitable land elsewhere as a reserve. If there is -any further provision that ought to be inserted in order to safeguard thoroughly the rights of the Indians, we will be very happy indeed to have suggestions in that regard. The object of the section is to extend along a certain line provisions which have already been sanctioned by Parliament and which in -some cases have been found not to be fully adequate to r>
oet considerations of the public interest.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I understand the
legislation it would be only under provisions set forth at the commencement of the section.

But it includes every Indian reserve.	For there is i no Indian reserve that floes not contain ' more land than is necessary for the use of the band '; no reserve is occupied so efficiently that it could not be (reasonably considered that there is room for more than the Indians to whom it is allotted. Then there is no Indian reserve of which it is not true that it ' materially retards the natural development of the surrounding country.' On these two counts every Indian reserve in Canada is subject to being decreased in iarea by reason of the order of the judge of the Exchequer Court; and the judge would have no option if j;he matter were brought to his attention.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But in the first place the proposal must commend itself to the minister, and he is responsible to Parliament, of course, for his action, and can be made amenable to Parliament if he exercises this power in an improvident or unjust manner. Then, after that the court must distinctly consider whether or not it is expedient that the band of Indians should be removed from that reserve.

I beg pardon, the courts
must decide simply whether there is more land than is necessary for the Indians.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will read to my hon.
friend what I was relying upon. It is provided that the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the superintendent gener al may-
__refer to the Exchequer Court of Canada for
inquiry and report the question as to whether it is expedient, having regard to the interest of the public and of the Indians of the band for whose use the reserve is held, that the whole or any portion of the said reserve should he sold for the benefit of the Indians, and that the Indians should be removed from the reserve or any part of it.
The judge of the Exchequer Court is to take that into consideration and report upon it. The minister, in the first place,
must decide that it is a proper case to refer to the court, and it is left to the judge of the Exchequer Court to determine whether it is expedient that the Indians should be removed. If he decides that they should he removed, provision must he made by Parliament and compensation must be afforded the Indians so that they may suffer no finarcjal loss.

I have listened very carefully to the debate, and 1 am more convinced than I was at first that this legislation is objectionable. I have in my constituency the Restigouche reserve, the oldest Micmac reserve in eastern Canada, and the centre of the missionary efforts among the Micmacs for eastern Quebec and the Maritime provinces. This reserve is located very close to the town of Campfoelltown. Now, from the white man's point of view the proximity of an Indian reserve to a town injures that town. That does not mean that therefore the Indians . must go. From the point of view of the white man the Indians are not using the whole of the land contained in their reserve. As a matter of fact they do not do much farming. Most of them act as guides in the summer foT American sportsmen who come to fish on the Restigouche and Cascapedia, and in the winter time they are in the shanties. For this reason, it would be found by the judge of the Exchequer Court, or by anyone else going there, that the Indians do not occupy all the land in their reserve.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How near are they to the town of Campbellton?

Just .across the river, only a few minutes' distance. And as to the material development of the surrounding country, from the white man's standpoint, for instance, the establishment of a pulp and paper factory or a saw-mill, and the employment of a lot of white men, would certainly mean the development of the country. But the Indians have been there for over a century and a half-close upon two centuries; and .if they are sent away under the terms proposed now a grave injustice will be done. The most objectionable part of the legislation, to my mind, is that we are not told who must make the application to the minister for this property. If the application were made by the missionary order, who have had in charge for generations the moral, religious, intellectual and every other interest of the Indians, or if the appli-

cation had to be made by the town council of Campbellton, a public 'body, declaring that the reserve .should he used for public purposes, it would not be so bad. But under this legislation any one could make the application, and we should not know who made it until it was acted upon by the minister who refers it to Council. Of course, reference has to be made by the Governor in Council to the judge of the Exchequer Court. The court must decide whether it is expedient that the band of Indians should be removed from the reserve or any part of it. Well, any number of witnessess from Campbellton would testify that it is to the interest of the town to get these Indians out of the way; it is obviously to the interest of the town that they should be removed. The interest of the white men is in favour of the establishment of a pulp mill which *would necessitate the removal of the Indians. But that is not necessarily a final reason why the Indians should be sent away from the reserve. The Indians have already conceded a portion of their reserve for a saw-mill, and I think they are getting along pretty well with the company, though they had some difficulty at first. But from rumours circulating in the county and district, well known to the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Reid) as well as to myself, an effort is being made to get possession of that reserve. If it were solely for the public interest, I would not have so much objection, but I am afraid it is going to be obtained for private interest rather than for the interest of the country. The Indians are well situated; they have a magnificent church, and they benefit by the labour of the splendid order of missionaries who are looking after their interests and who can do so much better for them in that locality than they could if the Indians were removed. For this reason, I cannot help being reminded of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and his bold, determined fight for the St. Peter's reserve. If it were made easier for these people to get these Indian reserves, they could easily invoke these reasons and the judge of the Exchequer Court would have to admit that the Indians have more land than they use and that their presence materially retards the advancement of the town and the surrounding country from the point of view of the white man. The decision is supposed to hinge upon ' whether it is in the interest of the public.' Of course, that is the white man s view of it-it is not in the interest of development from the white man's point

of view that the Indians should be there at all.
Section 6 says:
Having regard to the interests of the public and of the Indians of the band for whose use the reserve is held, that the whole or any portion of the said reserve should be sold for the benefit of the Indians, and that the Indians should be removed from the reserve or any part of it.
These things are easily established. Of course, the interests of the greatest number-the interests of the public-must overrule everything. If I were satisfied that in the application of this law nothing but the public interest would dominate; if applications under the Act were made by a reputable body, by the order of Capuchins, for instance, who are kloing missionary work among the Indians and who have their interests at heart, I would consider the legislation to be not half as bad as it might be; but if applications for Indian reserves, or portions of them, are to be made by ordinary companies for business purposes, all the provisions of this Bill can easily be complied with, and the report of the judge of the Exchequer Court given to the minister and to Parliament. Parliament will accept the report of the Exchequer Court judge, the legislation will be put through, and the Indians deprived of their reserve, and a great injustice will, in my opinion, be committed.

In this legislation I think there is no doubt about the safeguarding of the public interest. Sub-section 1 of section 6 says that:
The Governor in Council may refer to the Exchequer Court of Canada for inquiry and report the question as to whether it is expedient, having regard to the interests of the public and the Indians-
And so on. Subsection 4 says:
If the court finds that it is expedient that the band of Indians should be removed from the reserve.
I think that in order to safeguard the interests of the Indians, this subsection should say: ' having regard to the interests of the Indians and of the public.' After the Exchequer Court judge hears counsel and evidence on both sides, he might find it expedient, in the interests of the people, to send the Indians-out; according to the wording of this section he would be quite justified in doing so. But if the wor'ds in subsection 1 with regard to the interests of the Indians were inserted also in sub-

section 4, the interests' of the Indians would be thoroughly safeguarded.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Act in that respect has been copied precisely from the old Act, which was passed under the regime of the hon. member for Edmonton. There is some point, however, in what my hon. friend suggests, and I think that it could be met if after the word 'expedient' there were inserted the words 'as aforesaid.'

If the department employs solicitors to act for the Indians, great caution should he exercised by that solicitor to ascertain the exact facts that exist with regard to the particular bands of Indians whose reservations are to be taken over by the department. Application was made to two or three preceding governments to get the reserve of the Indians in the city of Sydney, which is a valuable piece of land. The Indians there live under peculiar conditions. The Micmacs of Nova Scotia earn their living generally by making tubs, baskets, and so on, but the Indians of the reserve in the city of Sydney make their living simply by labour, and if they were removed from Sydney-it certainly would be in the interests of the city of Sydney that they should be removed-their occupation would be practically gone. They have not taken up the occupation of their forefathers, and, if removed from Sydney, they would be taken away from the locality where they would ordinarily be able to make a living. I bring this matter up merely to show that great precautions should be taken by, and very detailed instructions given to the solicitors in each case with regard to the particular reserve in question. If all precautions are taken by the department, by agents and by solicitors, I would rather *see the Act administered by a judge of the Exchequer Court or of any other court than by any department of any government.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That the words ' as aforesaid ' be inserted after the word ' expedient ' in the first line of subsection 4 of section 6.
