stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell (Minister of Agriculture), Bill No. 113 to regulate
Cold Storage Warehouses was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the 'Chair.
On section 1-short title:

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The intention of this Bill
is to give statutory power to exercise what we may call reasonable and desirable control over the cold storage industry of the country in so far as it is connected with the food supply of the public. We thought it well to deal with it, if we deal with it at all, as a federal matter although it has been argued that it is more a matter of provincial concern. It has not been found to work v.ery well in those States of the Union that
have taken up the control of cold storage, and considering it more as a federal matter the Federal Government of the United States are now contemplating passing legislation in that direction. In the commerce connected with the food supplies of the whole country, cold storage, as every member of the House knows, is a factor of very recent importance, but of very extraordinary importance. I think possibly the best brief description of cold storage is this:
Cold storage is essentially the application of scientific temperature control to the solution of an economic problem, namely the storage of the surplus of one season against the want of the next and of preventing the fluctuation of prices from below the cost of production at harvest to a point beyond the resources of the purse the remainder of the year.
As every one knows, the problem of the preservation of food from one season to another, or from a period of flush production to a period of scarce production is as old as life itself, and it is only by the artificial control of temperatures in recent years that the whole question of cold storage has come so prominently to the front, and has made it a matter of very special public interest. To use the words of one writer:
Cold storage has enlarged the number of food products preservable to their original condition and created a new industry; it has largely removed the function of this class of food preservation from the scattered individual producers to large central establishments and thrown the business of accumulating and conserving surplus more fully into the hands of tradesmen. It has permitted the preservation of flesh foods in a raw state, which were never before so preservable; and it has so improved the quality of stored products whose current production never ceases entirely that in many cases the held goods cannot be distinguished from the fresh production.
I can only say for myself-mid I think most members who have given this matter any consideration will agree with me- that the history and development of the whole cold storage movement is a great, if not, perhaps, an unmixed blessing. Like other businesses closely concerned with popular needs, it has its evils. There is a tendency, of course, to centralization and specialization, and it is partly, I think, because of this, and partly because of the increase in the cost of living in recent years, that there has been a good deal of criticism levelled at cold storage, chiefly along two lines: first, along the line of prices, it being assumed, in some quarters, that extortionate prices by cold storage men have led to an increase in the cost of living-and, secondly, largely on account of a misconception, criticism has been

levelled against the health side of cold storage. It was on account of a lot of this criticism in the United States that various states put through legislation, some of it, however, not working out very well. It was only as recently as 1911 that the first state law was enacted in relation to cold storage-in the state of Indiana, I think it was. At the present time about eleven states have cold storage legislation, but there is no federal legislation. In a natural season of production, if we could assume that there was no such thing as the preserving of food products, the man who produces food does it first for himself, and then for the rest of the community. When their needs are supplied naturally the prices come down, and he is going to cease producing any more until prices give him at least some little profit for himself. Then comes a slack season of production and prices go up. Finally there is a season of no production, when prices amount to almost famine levels for any of the particular articles which are not produced at all. One might ask what is the actual effect of cold storage within the last ten or fifteen years on our modern commercial life. Briefly, I think I may put it in this way: That it enables the carrying of food products from a season of flush production to a time of no production or a minimum production, and trus has resulted in a lowering of prices, and also enables a greater production because the man who can produce for a relatively larger market is going to produce more heavily than ever before. I think it would ibe well within the mark to state in connection with the criticism of the high prices that cold storage men have exacted in this country, and in the United States, that on the whole prices have been lower for the whole year than they would have been if we had no cold storage at all. It has been said by some people that speculation has entered into this question, and that prices have been held up at an absolutely unreasonable height; but those who have given any study to the matter at all will find that although speculation has sometimes entered into it to a regrettable extent, taking one year, with another the man who goes into the cold storage business after all, perhaps, gets only a moderate profit. In this connection I would like to read a line or two of the report of the commission that was appointed some time ago by the Chicago Association of Commerce, which practi-
cally bears out the report of the Massachusetts committee, which probably gave more study to this question than any other committee. The commissioners say:
Exhaustive examination of the statistics compiled under the direction of your committee, and a comparison of these statistics with the facts obtained by the Department of Agriculture, after an exhaustive research demonstrates clearly that the prices of butter, eggs, poultry and fish have been more uniform during the year since cold storage has become a factor in the care of food products than before that period. These statistics also show that taking an average for a period of years, prices on the whole have been lower than during the years when cold storage was unknown.
Dr. H. E. Barnard, State Food and Drug Commissioner of Indiana, has said that this statement is in substantial agreement with the conclusions reached by the Massachusetts committee, and that it is undoubtedly an accurate gauge of the effect of cold storage upon the price of foodstuffs. A good deal of criticism has been levelled at cold storage in connection with its health phase. On this point I would like to quote from probably the greatest authority on the continent, Dr. Mary E. Pennington, who is chief of the United tates Food Research Laboratory. In the examination held recently she was asked this question:
How does the change that takes place at the end of twelve months of cold storage, 10 degrees F., compare with the change that takes Place in the same product after twenty-four hours' exposure under the same circumstances before refrigeration?
Dr. Pennington: There would probably he a greater change in twenty-four hours if the temperature was from 65 degrees to 75 degrees than if the temperature was 10 degrees F. for twelve months.
Mr. Littlefield: That is to say, the ordinary food product that is kept in the house, without being kept in a refrigerator, under ordinary circumstances would show more deterioration than the same food product kept in cold storage for twelve months?
Dr. Pennington: If the atmospheric temperature should be over 60 degrees, it would -that is in respect to chickens.-We have at the expiration of twelve months (in storage at 10 degrees F.) a change which is fairly comparable with the change at the end of fifteen days at 32 degrees F., and with the change at the end of five and a half days in a good house refrigerator, and which is very much less than the change at the end of three days at a temperature at from 65 to 75 degrees.
Senator Commins: As to meat kept hard frozen for twelve months; would a chicken so kept and eaten at the end of twelve months be injurious to the health of the person who ate it?
Dr. Pennington: I have eaten many of them and found them very palatable.
There has been a lot of discussion in regard to the effect of cold storage on eggs.
%

Dr. Pennington was- asked by a member of the .committee:
Will you be kind enough to say to the committee whether your results with reference to eggs are practically parallel with the results you have described in connection with poultry?
Dr. Pennington: The investigation or study of, eggs has been practically along the same lines as the study of poultry. Eggs are more difficult to handle if anything and keep in good condition than poultry. Nature has set a limit on eggs herself. An egg ordinarily will not keep in good condition under refrigeration for more than ten months-between nine and ten months generally-and it must be an extra good egg that will hold in good condition for ten months. Eggs that are to be kept under refrigeration must be even more carefully selected than poultry which is to be kept hard frozen.
In other places she repeats that am egg will deteriorate more in twenty-four hours in a certain condition of temperature and humidity than in eight or nine months in cold storage. One other illustration I might give of the result in regard to fish because it has been stated that the effect of cold storage on fish is rather disastrous. The testimony of Dr. William J. Gi-es, Professor of Biological Chemistry, Columbia University, is interesting in this regard. He was asked:
Mr. Littlefield: Have you had occasion to examine fish that have been the subject of cold storage?
Dr. Gies: I have.
Mr. Littlefield: Please state to the committee what your experiments in that line have been?
Dr. Gies: Briefly stated, fish In cold storage for a year, blue fish for example, and fluke- when allowed to thaw in my office on an ordinary table at room temperature after 24 hours; (that is after the fish had softened) appeared to be practically identical with fresh fish of the same kind.
I am only giving these instances to show that there is a great deal of misconception about the effect pf cold storage, from a health point of view, on food. The conclusion -arrived at by practically all the authorities who have looked into this matter is that a vastly greater effect is to be attributed to the condition of the food when it goes into cold storage than the length of time in which it stays in cold storage.
As to the legislation on the subject, there are eleven states of the union which have acts on their statute books, but as these acts have only been in existence for the past two and a-half years there has not been time to see how they have worked out. In Pennsylvania they have a law which has been very much quoted and it is not at all popular, not only with a great many of the
fruit producers and handlers but even with a good many portions of the public. In Massachusetts probably the law has worked out more satisfactorily, and I can give the committee roughly the lines upon which these cold storage bills run. We recently sent our cold storage commissioner, Mr. Buddick, down to Boston, to Pennsylvania and to New York to to get into contact with the people connected with the operation of the cold storage laws and study them as closely as he could, to talk with the leading people interested in cold storage matters and to obtain such information as he could for the benefit of any legislation which might be brought forward here. At the present time in Canada we have about forty-six public cold storages, twenty-seven of which have received subsidies, or are at present receiving them from the Government; that is thirty per cent on the cost of construction. In this country there are something like fifty private cold storage establishments, abattoirs and other places of that kind. As nearly as I can learn the total cold storage capacity in Canada would be about 18,000,000 to 20,000,000 cubic feet, a very small amount when it is realized that in the city of Boston alone they have one company which is operating about 10,000,000 cubic feet of cold storage. As far as the actual quantity of.food products going into cold storage both here and in the United States is concerned, I think that probably it would not amount to more than eight or ten per cent. As far as our own country goes, of course, the whole cold storage system is comparatively in the very beginning of its development. We have thought, therefore, that in this legislation it would be better not to fix any arbitrary limit of time, or to embody in the legislation some of the details that have been worked out in the state legislation across the line because they are continually altering their laws as they are found to be unsatisfactory. The whole thing is in an experimental stage and we thought that it would be better to ask the House to pass this Bill in such shape as to give power, by regulation, to deal with all the questions practically that have been dealt with in most of the legislation passed in the various states. I shall take the legislation in the States of Massachusetts and Pennsylvania as examples. In Pennsylvania they have an arbitrary time limit fixed during which food products may be kept in cold storage. It is provided that beef may be kept four months; pork, sheep, lamb, six months;

veal, three months; fowl, drawn, five months, undrawn, ten months; eggs, eight months; butter, nine months; fish, nine months. There are also certain regulations in regard to marking. The food or the container is to be marked with the date of receipt and withdrawal. The sale of food kept in cold storage outside of the state is prohibited if held for more than the time limit or unless marked as provided. Quarterly reports to the dairy and food commissioner are provided for and more frequently if required by such officer. In Massachusetts the law was approved on May 27 and it became effective on September 1, 1912. It includes fresh meat and fresh meat products, fresh fish, poultry, eggs and butter. There is a time limit of tmelve months which may be extended by the state board of health if the foods are still in good condition. Articles of food, except fish, or container, are to be marked with the date of receipt. Reports are to be made quarterly to the state board of health or more frequently if the board requires.
In various states they require from three to four reports a year to a yearly report. In this Bill we have provided, under section 4, that the regulations will deal with all these questions including the question of making returns to the Government to show exactly what is in cold storage. I think that, without wearying the committee any more as to the general lines upon which the Bill runs, I will leave the committee to take it up clause by clause.
Would the minister explain how he will control importations ex cold storage from other countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have not worked out that feature, and I cannot say just now exactly how the United States is dealing with that.

The minister proposes to fix a time limit on cold storage in Canada, but supposing stuff had been in colld storage in Massachusetts fpr eight months and was then shipped to Canada, how is he going to help that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am not definitely proposing that we should exercise the power now to impose a time limit, and I am not sure it would be wise to do so with our present knowledge. In the Bill we are reserving the power to fix a time limit if our experience should justify the department in doing so. As to other stuff coming from cold storage to Canada, I presume

that would be dealt with under the inspection of food.	.

The certificate given by the minister to cold storage and its operation would rather lead to the conclusion that there was no necessity for this Bill. Cold storage as carried on at present, as I would gather from the remarks of the minister, is altogether a benevolent and generally a beneficent institution. That being the case there does not seem to be any serious necessity for its regulation. I think the majority of the House will believe that notwithstanding the good opinion the minister has of cold storage, the principle of cold storage an'd its operation, its regulation by the authority of Parliament is entirely desirable. The principle which the minister announces as being the principle of cold storage, namely, that by this means the surplus of one season can be made to supply the scarcity of the following season to the benefit of the consumer and producer in both seasons, is a beautiful theory, but like many other theories it does not work out in practice. As a matter of fact, everybody believed when cold storage was begun that it was going to work exactly in the way the minister suggested, namely, that the producer was going to get more and the consumer was going to pay less, but after the experience of several years the general public have come to the conclusion that the way cold storage works out is that the consumer pays more and the producer gets less. It is generally believed now that the policy of holding perishable food products from season to season enables the dealer on a large scale in these products, who has cold storage facilities, to control the market both as to purchase and sale, as he could not do unless he had the facilities of cold storage. It is believed that as a matter of fact, having that control of the market, he uses the control to depress unduly the price to the producer by reason of his always having an available surplus on hand, and on the other hand to unduly enhance the cost to the consumer because he can always hold back the supply without it being destroyed by process of time. It is because of this condition, the very opposite of the theory which the minister places before the House, that regulation under Government authority becomes a necessity. While I do not agree with the minister's premises I do agree with his conclusion.
But while we want governmental regulation we want that regulation on the authority and with the knowledge of Parliament, as a

means by which the public is aware of what is being done for its benefit. The minister has taken authority to do as he pleases in regard to the regulation of cold storage; in regard to the regulation of the. supply and demand of a large percentage of the food of the people, without reference to any authority except his own will and that of his colleagues in the Cabinet. That is a fairly large order and for my own part I do not think it is an order that should be filled. 1 think that in all fairness, the Government if satisfied that regulation of such an important department of business and of life is necessary, should be prepared to inform the public through the medium of Parliament how far they propose to go in that regulation. The fact still remains that cold storage ought to be a public benefit, and it is by means of legislation that we hope to secure that benefit to the public that we do not secure at the present time. Before we give authority to the minister, we would like to know how far the interests of the public are to be protected, if they are to be protected; how far the present conditions of monopoly are to be affected; whether they are to be perpetuated, or whether the interests of the public are to be left in the condition they are in to-day. It is not a small matter; it is a very great matter, and I and others think that before the Government ask for such wide authority they should be in a position to inform the House to what extent they expect to exercise that authority, and in fact to, so far as possible, take authority direct from Parliament so that the public would know how far they are being protected and how far they are not. I think legislation on the subject is-entirely desirable, but I think it is altogether too much in line with about ninety-nine per cent of the legislation brought down by this Government since it took office; that is to say, legislation giving authority to govern by Order in Council. That is necessary at times, but I am one to say that I think we have had really too much of it at the hands of this Government, and I regret that this is another example.
Will this Bill cover the cold storage of meat ?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, it covers all cold storage.

There are regulations now providing that an inspector shall be in every cold storage warehouse where meats are put in cold storage. Is it the purpose of this Bill that a regulation shall be made that there shall be a Government inspector in every cold storage warehouse ?
If so, I woulid suggest to the minister that the certificate of the inspector should be prima facie evidence that the product was fit for food when it entered that warehouse. Otherwise the burden oi proof would be on the party who put the goods into storage and the goods might not be put into cold storage at all on receipt and might be spoiled before being put into cold storage. The consequence would be that, if the goods were spoiled, the burden of proof would be on the man who put them in. He would have no evidence at all; all the evidence would be in the hands of the cold storage warehouse. If he had a suit, if the goods were spoiled through the fault of the cold storage warehouse, he would have to call as witness a man in charge of that warehouse, and probably the man who handled the goods when they went in could not be found. Therefore, I would suggest-and I think this is a provision that is in the cold storage bills in other places, especially in the United States-that a certificate of the Government inspector, where there is an inspector in a warehouse in this country, should be prima facie evidence that the goods were as he certified that they were when they went in, that is fit for human food.
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER: I do not rise to make any extended remarks, but the subject under consideration is one which is of peculiar interest. I apprehend that we are considering question 4?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on section 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
(reading):
3.	The Governor in Council may make such regulation as he deems necessary or expedient, to provide for a supervision of all cold storage warehouses.
4.	Such regulations may provide,-
(a)	for the licensing of all cold storage warehouses;
(b)	for the inspection of all cold storage warehouses;
(c)	for a system of periodic and other reports by owners of cold storage warehouses showing the quantities in storage of the several articles of food.
In regard to that, it appears to me that the report made by the owners should be a report not only as to the quantities in storage of the several articles of food, but as to the time they are in cold storage. It seems to me that the time articles of food are kept in cold storage is of paramount, importance to the consuming public of this country. I notice that the minister made reference in his remarks to eggs being kept

ten months in cold storage. Personally I am not an expert as to how long an egg should !be kept in cold storage; but from some little experience I have had with eggs that" have been in cold storage for five or six months, I would say that a period of ten months was absolutely too long. In support of that contention I propose to give the House some information elicited last fall during an investigation into the high cost of articles of food by a committee appointed by the United States Government, which sat in the city of New York during the month of November. At this investigation some very startling evidence was brought to light as to the method and management and the result of cold storage systems operated in the United States. It seems to me that what is true of large cities in the United States may be equally true of cities in Canada where cold storage has been adopted or put into force to the same degree. The committee sat not only in New York but in other large cities of the United States, and the conditions they found there were similar. At the possible expense of wearying the House, I should like to put on ' Hansard ' a few of the findings of that committee during their session in New York.
About that time one of the leading newspapers took up the question and showed it up to the public in a very remarkable manner. Demonstration stations were opened in various parts of the cities after the results of the investigation were brought to light, so that eggs that had formerly been selling on the market for 45, 50 and 60 cents per dozen were actually placed on the market at these demonstration stations at the price of thirty-two cents per dozen. In discussions which I had with egg dealers and other gentlemen closely connected with this business, I was informed, much to my surprise, that what had been brought to light at that investigation was going on and had been going on for a great number of years. One of the leading newspapers, the Globe, came out on November 2, as follows-I will read just a quotation or two:
Everybody in New York now knows that the public is being robbed by the egg gamblers, but everybody does not know th&L trie State of New York has conspired to help the gamblers in their cold-blooded conspiracy against public health and the public pocketbook. The Globe proposes through this demonstration station at the corner of 8th avenue and 121st street to make the whole scheme of egg trickery, egg fraud and egg corruption so transparent that the authorities, who now say they never realized what was going on, will no longer have any excuses for inaction, and that the people may 
have sufficient facts within their hands to enable them to give themselves the protection which they are now denied by the national, state and city governments. The eggs which will be sold [DOT]to-morrow in the Globe demonstration station at 32 cents per dozen are nothing more nor less than storage eggs. There are no ' fresh eggs ' in New York.
According to the Globe there were no fresh eggs in New York on November 2. That seems to be a startling thing in itself. (Beading):
All the eggs sold in this city at the present time are known to the trade as ' western fresh,' ' fresh held ' and * storage.' Western fresh eggs may be from a month to three months old. Fresh held are between four and six months old. Storage eggs are between five and eight months old.
*So that when we come to consider the labelling of eggs for cold storage in Canada, I would respectfully draw to the attention of the minister that he pay particular attention to the framing of his regulations in that regard. (Beading):
One year ago we had a law that obliged the retailer to mark all ' storage ' eggs for just what they were. The people were eating storage eggs then just as they are eating them now, but they did not know the facts then as they do now. Therefore when they saw the word ' storage ' on the egg, they refused to buy it. At least this is what the egg gamblers, who held the eggs in storage, said to the New York Legislature, and the New York Legislature believed the story and at once repealed the law so that the retailer could label his storage eggs with a lie and call them 'fresh.' Under this fraudulent * fresh ' label the public is content to pay as high as 55 cents or 60 cents per dozen for the same'eggs for which it would not pay 35 cents per dozen if they sold under their correct name. So say the egg gamblers, whose influence was so powerful with New York politicians that quietly and obligingly the politicians changed the law.
Back to the demonstration station eggs, everyone of which is guaranteed to he a good egg of the class known as ' straight candled storage.'
I point out these words as the various degrees of eggs placed upon the market and eaten by the consumer. (Beading):
All the ' weak ' eggs, ' very weak ' eggs,
' spots,' and ' cracks ' have been candled out of these 32 cent storage eggs. Each case contains an average of from twenty to twenty-two dozen fancy and from eight to ten dozen fancy seconds. These are the same eggs that are now selling all over New York city at 40. 42, 45, 50 and 55 cents per dozen under labels that deceive.
As a matter of fact, they should sell to the public for much less than 32 cents per dozen. The Globe does not own them, however, and, therefore, cannot control the prices. These eggs were put away in storage in the month of June and at that time cost between 18 and 19 cents a dozen. Storage charges cost 40 cents per case, interest 22 cents per case, cartage 3 cents,

insurance 6 cents, which bring up the extra charges 71 cents per case of thirty dozen each.
At 19 cents per dozen, the outside price, a case of thirty dozen eggs when it went into storage cost If 5.70.
Plus the extra charges of 71 cents, these eggs now represent an investment of $6.41 per case of thirty dozen, or 21 1-3 cents per dozen. This figure, 21 1-3 cents per dozen, represents the actual money invested in each dozen of eggs which will be sold to-morrow at the Globe's demonstration station at 32 cents per dozen.
On November 1 there were 1,800,000 cases of storage eggs in New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, Boston, and Jersey city, representing an investment of $6.41 per case or $11,538,000. The gamblers who put these eggs away in the public coolers are now releasing them to the jobber at prices ranging from 29 cents to 40 cents per dozen. At a low estimate. The Globe takes the gambler's average price to the jobber at 30 cents per dozen, or $9 per case.
At this price the gambler realizes on the eggs held by him November 1, $16,200,000, or a profit of nearly $5,000,000. The jobber in selling these eggs to the retailer makes anothei profit of 2, 3, and 4 cents per dozen. At 2 cents per dozen his profit on a case is 60 cents. On 1,800,000 cases his profit is more than $1,000,000. The eggs which will be sold to-morrow at the Globe demonstration station at 32 cents per dozen were purchased from an egg gambler at 29 cents. Allowing the jobber a cent a dozen as his profit and also allowing him the loss on rejected eggs not good enough to sell at the demonstration station, the figure of 32 cents per dozen is arrived at.
At this price for good eggs the public allows a profit to those who have candled their eggs since November 1 of $5,742,000, which is exactly 50 per cent on the investment, quite a handsome figure. However, at 32 cents per dozen the public cannot buy good eggs in tne city of New York. As a matter of fact, many of the eggs sold at 45, 50 and 55 cents are not good eggs.
If we take the average retail price of eggs on sale to-day in New York at 45 cents per dozen, we have a retail value of $13.50 per case. At this price the eggs, which, with all over head charges figured into the cost, represent an investment of $11,538,000 now have a value of $24,300,000, showing a profit on one of the most necessary and vital articles of our daily food supply of over one hundred per cent.
In view of the facts elicited by that committee, I am bound to say that I agree absolutely with the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). While I have no fear in regard to trusting the Minister of Agriculture to draft regulations, and while I do not object to the Governor in Council making such regulations, I do feel that if Canada is to branch out into cold storage, as this Bill provides, the minister must make absolutely stringent regulations for the control of these articles of food; for in the future of this country the great difficulty we are going to have, and that wef have to-day, is perhaps not so much the| production of a food supply, but the dis-| tribution of that food supply, so as to get it| 225
from the producer to the consumer .at the lowest possible cost to the consumer, eliminating the various profits that are made to which profits the cold-storage of the .United States and of other countries, and I dare say of this country, will contribute ,a very large proportion. It is for that reason that I have risen to say that I hope that in any regulations enacted provision will be made for the owners to make a jeport with regard to the time these eggs .are to be in cold storage. Because after they are in there for several months, they ,are sorted out and graded under different names. Some axe a shade better than others. And, while there is a fine under the existing laws of New York for the selling of eggs of an inferior quality, and white, during the investigation of this committee, three men were actually put in jail for that offence, yet safeguards must ;be placed around the labelling of these eggs and the time they are in .cold-storage, in order do preserve the best interest of the consuming public of Canada. And if the minister had done no more to assist consumer and producer than the production of this measure-and he has done a great deal more, as every one will admit- he will have conferred upon the people of this country one of the greatest benefits that have ever been enacted by this House or that could have been conferred upon the people, because it means that he wi.l have the control of cold storage absolutely within his own power.

The Bill before the
House is a rather important one from any point of view, but I am forced to say is rather a makeshift Bill. When cold storage was first made a business in this country, the majority of the consumers in Canada were led to believe that it was going to be a blessing, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton. But as time went on, these cold-storage institutions, especially in our large cities, took upon themselves absolute monopoly over all the products they could handle that were necessary for the people of those cities, and as a distributing centre for the smaller towns and cities. In the large cities to-day of Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and others, these cold storage institutions will buy up foodstuffs such as meats, cheese, and so on when they are cheap, and will hold them there until other supplies have run out, and then they will take their own good Jltime to give these articles to the public as Ifresh articles at greatly enhanced prices. 1

356ft

would like to point out that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) introduced into this House a Bill which to my mind was almost a masterpiece of the legislation of the kind we should have in this country for the regulation of cold storage. There is very little use in the minister or the Government taking power to pass regulations governing this thing. The minister tells us, as I understand him, that there is no great necessity at present, and he does1 not see that there will be any in the near future, for placing a time limit for articles kept in cold storage. I say that is the most important point the minister must grapple with. I say that this feature which he thinks will not he needed now or in the near future is one of the most necessary features of legislation for the regulation of cold storage.
Articles are sent out of cold storage and solid to the unsuspecting public as fresh products. I say that every article put into cold storage should be handled in such a way that the consumer of that article would know exactly what he is buying. He should know, in the first place, whether or not the article is a cold storage article, and he should know, in the second place, how long it has been in cold storage. The question asked by the hon. member for Huntingdon is a very important one; I notice that it is covered by section 4 of the Bill introduced in this House by the hon. member for Selkirk, which says:
No food which has been placed in cold storage and has been removed therefrom for the purpose of sale shall be returned into cold storage.
The Bill brought down by the Minister of Agriculture makes absolutely no attempt to deal with that phase of the question. For example, articles which have been in cold storage in New York for seven, eight, nine or ten months may be sent to Canada and placed in cold storage here for a similar or a longer period of time. I think that there should be added to this Bill a section which would prohibit cold storage people in any other country or in any other part of Canada from removing their goolds from one cold storage warehouse to another with any other purpose in view than that of immediate sale and immediate distribution.
Another provision which, to my mind, should be in this Bill, is that which is embodied in section 9 of the Bill introduced by the hon. member for Selkirk. It is as follows:
All food taken out of cold storage and offered for sale shall be marked with a card upon which shall be plainly printed in red block let-
[Mr. Carroll, j
ters not less than two inches long, upon a white ground, the words 'cold storage goods.'
That would be notice to the public that instead of buying what they might suppose to be fresh goods, they were actually buying cold storage goods. I say that the Bill as introduced by the hon. Minister of Agriculture having regard to the fact that he has told us that at the present stage there is no necessity for a time limit and that we may, therefore, presume that no regulations will be made by the department to that end- is an absolutely bald Bill, and I do not think it should be allowed to pass unless there are incorporated in it some of the provisions which are contained in the Bill presented to the House by the hon. member for Selkirk. There is no doubt that if the Department of Agriculture will at the present stage embody in the present Bill the provisions contained in Bill 6, the proposed legislation will have some effect. In my humble opinion, the high cost of living in our large industrial centres to-day is traceable largely to cold storage in this country. The New York commission referred to by the hon. member for Kings has come to that conclusion. By putting legislation on our statute books which would force the co!d storage institutions in this country to break up their trusts, monopolies, and combines in respect of the necessaries of life, the minister would be giving relief to the consumers and incidentally not hurting the producers. While cold storage is of some benefit to the producers of foodstuffs, it is not the blessing to them that we were led to believe it would be when cold storage was given an impetus in this country by legislation some years ago. There can be no political controversy with regard to this piece of legislation. There are hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House who will think that the hon. minister's way of regulating cold storage warehouse is the better way, but I am sure that persons who have given attention and study to this subject will invariably tell the minister that instead of making regulations five, six and seven
11	p.m. months hence, we should have upon our statute books at the close of the present session such legislation as will contain every possible regulation having in view the interests of the people. The most stringent legislation with regard to the time during which goods may be kept in cold storage warehouses should be made. I think the minister would be well advised if he would revise his legislation and, instead of making regulations by Order in Council, regulate this

matter by provisions incorporated in this Bill and passed by this Parliament. I do not think that the minister, even in his own department, can get more information in the matter of cold storage than he oan get right here in the Chamber of the Commons. Here we- have gentlemen from all over the country-from the Maritime provinces, from central Canada and from the West. We are sent here to legislate, not to give power to the Government or to a member of a Government to make regulations. There are here members who have given this matter special consideration; members from all parts of Canada who know the conditions, and I am sure that after a thorough discussion of this Bill in the House the minister would come to the conclusion to pass a Bill not giving him power to make regulations but putting upon the statute book the regulations proposed by the hon. member for 'Selkirk.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It would depend entirely upon how far we went as far as regulations 'are concerned. I entirely agree with the view of the hon. member for South Cape Breton that this is not a political matter; we are all engaged in trying to do something towards effecting reasonable control and supervision of cold storage warehouses, which have never been subject to such supervision or control. But, with all due deference to the hon. member for Edmonton and to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, I must say that I do not entirely agree with all that they have said.
Our own cold storage commissioner has given this subject more attention than probably any member of this House. It is his particular business; he has had made a careful study of the question, and has looked into the matter at first hand as it exists in the United States,, and in view of the experiences that they had in the United States and the experience we had in our own department, we came to the deliberate conclusion that it would be at least a step in advance to warn all cold storage warehouses that we were going to demand from them a proper report of all their proceedings, and a right to inspect the condition of their warehouses in order to exercise some control over the stuff that went in and came out. That, in itself, would mean 225i
something; and I think it would be better to undertake that initial step and take power to make further regulations than, in the light of our present knowledge, to embody in a Bill things that might prove most unsatisfactory, very unworkable, and very cumbrous, and that would have to be dealt with over again. I believe that it is better to go slowly. I admit that it may not be always good policy to legislate by regulation. I quite appreciate that point of view, although I think my hon. friends opposite will agree that there has been a good deal of legislation for a great many years in which power has been taken to do things by regulation. That practice is not confined to this Government, and I do not suppose that any hon. member will assert that it is. I quite agree that something ought to be done, and I think it would be as foolish to do nothing as to go too far. I would .ask that this thing be given a trial. What I wanted to do was to refer this matter to the Agricultural Committee, who could examine witnesses, take evidence, and thresh the whole thing out. If the House comes to the conclusion that it would be better to do that-better to defer action until the matter has been thoroughly threshed out-I would prefer doing that than, in the light of my present knowledge, embodying in actual legislation at the present time a lot of the suggestions that have been made. As far as the Government is concerned, we have no desire except to do something towards exercising' proper supervision and control. After all,
I think that a great many cold storage v arehouses in the country are trying to do the square thing by the public, and I think that on the whole our system works out better than that of the United States, because although it is true that there are private institutions which may perhaps be engaged in a certain line of work that may-be called monopoly, at the same time we have a great number of cold storage warehouses of smaller capacity that exercise a reasonable check on them. Our system, initiated by the late Government, of .subsidizing a number of cold storage firms all over the country with a reasonable check on rates, has been spoken of in the highest terms by the United States authorities as being a step in the right direction, and as being a set off against monopolies controlling the cold storage business. My desire as minister, and the desire of the Government, is to take power, which we will exercise as fast as we can in the light of fuller knowledge,

and to demand, now, ? thorough accounting and reporting from cold storage warehouses, and to have such powers of inspection that we can make them toe the mark and see that all the stuff comes in and goes out properly. Some such step, we think, is in the public interest.

I am afraid I cannot altogether agree with the minister when he practically points out that the cold storage system of Canada and the United States has done so much good, and very little harm. I am one that believes the cold storage system is a blessing, if properly managed. If not properly controlled, I believe it may be one of the greatest curses ever inaugurated. From my own observations and I have given a little time to the study of this question-I am satisfied that something [DOT]ought to be done to control the cold storage systems of Canada. There is no question in my mind that under the present system-with no regulations at all-the cold storage systems of Canada can, and are storing away food products in the seasons of the year when they are flush, and holding them until the supply is scarce, and then exacting undue profits from the masses of the people of this country. I am satisfied of that. Take the present time for instance. April and May is the season when the eggs for the whole year are stored. Now the mere fact that the cold storage systems of the United States and Canada are in the market purchasing those eggs by the million, enchanees the price of eggs at the present time to the consumers of this country. The eggs are placed in cold storage and carried over till next winter when we are asked to pay double and sometimes treble the price that the cold storage people are paying for the eggs at the present time. The eggs were bought at the minimum price in April and May, although the price at that time was raised to the consumer because, if the cold storage people were not in the market for them, the eggs could be bought much cheaper.
Does my hon. frienld not think that the price would be higher six months from now, if there were no cold storage system?

No, I do not think the price would be higher, and I will tell you why. The consumer would be laying away the eggs as he used to in the old days, putting them away just as the cold storage people are doing now. They would not be cold storage eggs, but stored eggs, which

would be practically just as good for the average housekeeper.

Do the coM storage
people prohibit that now?

No, they do not; but the fact of the cold storage people being in the market has raised the price of eggs at this season of the year.
Mr. NESIBiITT: What about the producer? I am one of them.

That is all right; the producer is getting the benefit; but surely the consumer ought to be considered. The same thing applies to all food products; to meats, to fish, and everything that is put away in cold storage. I claim that the Bill that should be enacted as law in this country should make some provision for a time limit. The minister's Bill takes powers to regulate, and no doubt if the regulations limit the time of cold storage properly that would cover the necessities of the case, but everything depends on what those regulations are going to be. I have made a little attempt at framing a Bill for this purpose. I introduced a Bill in the early part of the session-
A very good one.

-but it did not get very far. I have given considerable attention to that Bill, and I believe it covers the essential points in a cold storage Bill for Canada. Clause 3 of my Bill was designed to give the minister control of the coM storage business of Canada; to license every firm in Canada doing a cold storage business; that no building could be utilized for cold storage purposes until it had been licensed by the Department of Agriculture. At the present time, there is absolutely no control. Any one can set up in the cold storage business and take in eggs, meat, and poultry, whether the cold storage house is sanitary or otherwise. If we are going to have a system of cold storage in Canada, I claim that it should be controlled absolutely by this Government, and we have a precedent for that. Eleven or twelve states on the other side of the line have been devoting a good deal of time in the last four or five years to legislation to controlthe cold storage systems of the United States. There has been a great deal done and there has been a great deal of money expended in the way of investigation. Many state committees, and some federal committees, have investigated this question thoroughly and we have a vast amount of evidence from all these committees which tends to

guide us in any legislation that we may pass here. California has a cold storage system [by license, also (Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York and North Dakota. In all these states there is legislation under which no cold storage system can exist except by procuring a license from the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
They will be licensed
here.

I am assured by the minister that they will be licensed here. That is an important point. Clause 4 of the Bill that I had before the House was designed to protect the health of the consumer. It is an established fact that ptomaine poisoning may occur from the . eating of meats, poultry and fish, not from the fact that they have been held in cold storage, but from the fact that it had been exposed to the atmosphere, thawed or partially thawed and then put back into cold storage and refrozen. All the authorities on hygiene who have studied this question agree that food should not be returned to cold storage after being exposed for sale in the open air. In nearly every one of the states to which I have referred it was enacted that no food products, taken out of cold storage and offered for sale, should be returned to cold storage again. All the evidence that I have under my hand, including that of Dr. Wiley, the celebrated American authority on this question, proves beyond doubt that many serious cases of ptomaine poisoning have been occasioned Iby the thawing out of poultry which has been taken out of cold storage, exposed in the butcher store or in the green-grocer's store for from one to three days, put back into cold storage, refrozen and offered for sale again. I provided in the Bill I had before the House that it should be illegal for a storekeeper to expose poultry or meats for-sale which had been taken out of cold storage and then to place these products back in cold storage and have them refrozen.
Clause 5 of my Bill was designed for the purpose of informing the public as to how long meat and other food products had been held in cold storage. That is a clause that is contained in the Act of every state to which I have referred. It is provided that every product offered for sale should be labelled ' cold storage food,' ' cold storage eggs,' or 'cold storage meat,' so that the consumer, when he walks into the store and
purchases any article, will know what he is buying. My hon. friend from Kings, Nova Scotia0(Mr. A. DeWitt Foster), has given us some information as to the effect this has had in New York. Evidence given before the committee of the United States Senate shows that cold storage eggs are sold repeatedly as fresh eggs in New York city.
It is done right here in Ottawa and in every city in Canada. People imagine that they are buying fresh eggs when they are paying from 50 to 75 cents per dozen, but as a matter of fact they are buying cold storage eggs. It is the duty of the Government to have these eggs labelled when they come out of cold storage. Nobody objects to eating a cold storage egg, if good, as the cold storage egg may be just as good as the fresh egg, but we do object to paying the price of fresh eggs when we are getting cold storage eggs. It would be a very simple thing to have a law passed that would compel those who deal in eggs or meat to have these articles labelled as being cold storage products.
Clause 6 was designed to protect the consumer in two ways: The first was to make it impossible for large cold storage plants to corner any sort of food products and by doing so increase the cost to the consumer. The second was to ensure as far as possible that the product mentioned to be sold was in prime condition. This, Mr. Chairman, is a very important clause. If cold storage operators are allowed to hold eggs for an indefinite time the effect is liable to be very disastrous to the consumer. We have records showing that eggs have been held as long as three years and then sold to the consumer. We have evidence here, taken by the committee to which I have referred, demonstrating clearly that after three weeks eggs begin to deteriorate. If the egg is put into the cold storage perfectly fresh and the temperature is maintained regularly at from 32 to 34 F., they say that an egg will keep for six months perfectly fresh but we know by experience that we eat eggs in Ottawa that have been in cold storage from eight to twelve months and sometimes longer. The egg loses its value as a food product. The same applies to meat. You can hold meat, if it is put into a sanitary cold storage in prime condition, properly frozen and kept frozen, for a considerable time, but no one can tell me that meat does not deteriorate after it has been frozen. Take a quarter of beef out of cold storage and expose it to the atmosphere and the deterioration is . so rapid that it soon becomes unfit to eat. But that is not the worst feature of it to my mind. I believe
How would you pay for that cold storage?

I would propose that the Government should pay a large proportion of the cost, and that the producers in the different localities should pay the balance. We are bonusing now large cold storage warehouses to the extent of twenty per cent, and we could afford I believe, to bonus these smaller places to the extent of 50 per cent, and that it would be in the interest of the consumers and producers alike. The producer, I believe, will obtain a better price for his products and the con-

sumer "would obtain these products at a less price than he is paying to-day, (because there would be eliminated the cold storage middlemen, who take these eggs and hold them for months, and then ask and get a bigger price than they ought to. It seems to me that something along this line should be done by the Government.
The high cost of living is a live question throughout the country, and we have had it discussed in this House. It is well known that there is no country in the world that has a better supply of fresh fish than we *have. Canada is one of the greatest fish-producing countries 'in the world, and yet you find that the people of Canada are paying to-day more for their fish than are the people of any other country similarly situated. On the Atlantic coast we have one of the greatest fisheries in the world, and on the Pacific coast we have enormously productive halibut grounds. We have allowed these halibut grounds to be exploited by the Americans. Last year 26,000,000 pounds of that fish were shipped from the Pacific coast, principally to the United States. I claim that, through a proper cold storage system, controlled by the Government, we ought to be able to in some way control a fair proportion of the halibut for sale in Canadian cities at a reasonable price, and the same would apply to the products of our Atlantic fisheries. A few days ago in this House some gentlemen from the Lower provinces urged the Government to subsidize a line of steamers to take our fish to Boston, but .it seems to me a more sensible and practical thing, and more in the interests of the consumers of Canada, would be to provide cheap transport for fish from the Atlantic coast to Ontario and Manitoba, so that we would be able to purchase this fish at a reasonable cost, instead of bonusing a line of steamers to take it out of our country. These are problems we have to face, and problems that require a great deal of study and thought. We have these great natural resources which belong to the people of ,Canada, and the people of Canada have the right to get the full benefit of them. Instead of encouraging the export of our natural products such as fish, it would be much better to encourage interprovincial means of transportation, so that the people of Canada might be supplied with Canadian fish at a reasonable cost.
There is just one other phase of the question. I am not going to take up any more of the time of the House; but I shall be very glad to see this Bill go into force,
and I hope, when it does, that every cold storage system of Canada will be placed under the absolute control of the (department; that it will be licensed, and that every one of these cold storage systems will be compelled to make a monthly report of the amount of food products of different kinds held in the different cold storage plants. I believe this is absolutely necessary in the interest of the public. The public should know how many eggs and how much meat are at a given time in the cold storage systems of the country. If the public knew that, it would go a long way perhaps towards compelling the cold storage people, the people who control the food products of this country, to do the right thing by the people. The trouble at the present time is that there are millions of dozens of eggs and millions of pounds of meat stored away sometimes for one, two or three years. The people Ido not know it; and the cold storage people have been known to take out tons and tons of chicken and poultry of different kinds that have been in cold storage for two or three years and have destroyed them sooner than sell them to the people at a reasonable price at a reasonable time. I hope the minister will take every precaution he can to safeguard the interest of the people.
